    22	discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
    23	In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
    24	principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
    25	cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
    26	using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
    27	has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
    28	record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
    29	mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.
    30	
    31	The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
    32	cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
    33	hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
    34	If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
    35	replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
    36	important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
    37	Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
    38	state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
    39	specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
    40	conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
    41	not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
    42	lemma was applied.
    43	
    44	The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
    45	policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
    46	notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
    47	prose.
    48	
    49	\section{Concision and Readability}
    50	
    51	A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
    52	in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
    53	uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
    54	checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
    55	\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
    56	formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
    57	implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
    58	and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.
    59	
    60	The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
    61	\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
    62	reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
    63	source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
    64	and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
    65	derivation genuinely needs room.
    66	
    67	Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
    68	special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
    69	equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
    70	avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
    71	blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
    72	forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
    73	belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.
    74	
    75	If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
    76	stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
    77	If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
    78	the issue or pull request in a footnote.
    79	
    80	\section{When the Investigation Starts}
    81	
    82	The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
    83	than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
    84	that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
    85	statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
    86	hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
    87	the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
    88	argument.
    89	
    90	The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
    91	after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
    92	already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
    93	inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
    94	formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
    95	relevant files already compile.
    96	
    97	At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
    98	local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
    99	intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
   100	missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
   101	the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
   102	real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
   103	formalized.
   104	
   105	A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
   106	not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
   107	mathematics.
   108	
   109	Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
   110	the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
   111	existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
   112	These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
   113	such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
   114	describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
   115	note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
   116	mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
   117	implementation.
   118	
   119	\section{When to Write a Note}
   120	
   121	A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
   122	match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
   123	estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
   124	conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
   125	identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
   126	probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
   127	a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
   128	between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
   129	relation.
   130	
   131	A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
   132	source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
   133	bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
   134	declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
   135	and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
   136	plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
   137	form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
   138	removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
   139	\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.
   140	
   141	Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
   142	\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
   143	not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
   144	necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.
   145	
   146	When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
   147	argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
   148	bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
   149	development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
   150	proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
   151	though it were the paper theorem.
   152	
   153	This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
   154	a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
   155	and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
   156	in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
   157	boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
   158	argument.
   159	
   160	A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
   161	intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
   162	inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
   163	argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
   164	final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
   165	theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
   166	cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
   167	should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
   168	says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
   169	and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
   170	cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
   171	should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.
   172	
   173	\section{Counterexamples}
   174	
   175	If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
   176	that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
   177	smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
   178	should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
   179	the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.
   180	
   181	When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
   182	especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
   183	otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
   184	whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
   185	of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
   186	a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
   187	still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.
   188	
   189	\section{Revision of a Note}
   190	
   191	A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
   192	obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
   193	revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
   194	declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
   195	classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
   196	which point remains unsettled.
   197	
   198	Later revisions should not make the note into a chronological log.  They should
   199	rewrite the document so that it remains a coherent account of the present
   200	mathematical understanding.  If the verdict changes, the conclusion should state
   201	the current verdict; the linked issue or pull request can preserve the earlier
   202	discussion.
   203	
   204	\section{Form of the Note}
   205	
   206	Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant
   207	source article, and provide enough traceability for the reader to locate the
   208	original passage and the project discussion.  GitHub issues and pull requests may
   209	be linked with \verb|\href|, and source files, line ranges, and labels should be
   210	recorded when they help the reader check the claim.  These references should
   211	serve the exposition rather than govern it: the main text should be organized
   212	around the mathematical assertion and its proof.
   213	
   214	The note should introduce its notation before using it.  Symbols for
   215	measurements, tensor factors, approximation relations, and error parameters
   216	should be named in prose.  If an approximation relation is state-dependent, the
   217	state should be named, or its defining expression should be given when this can
   218	be done briefly.  Only after the notation is in place should the note state the
   219	assertion in the cited source, using a bibliographic citation such as
   220	\verb|\cite[Section~...]{...}| when the section or chapter is known.
   221	
   222	Only the relevant hypotheses should be reproduced.  If the question is a scalar
   223	substitution, a missing term, or a missing hypothesis, the note should not quote
   224	a long unrelated part of the proof.  It should give the cited lemma or
   225	proposition in the special case actually used, then display the calculation or
   226	logical implication in which the discrepancy appears.
   227	
   228	Displayed equations should be used with restraint.  They are appropriate for the
   229	source estimate being checked, the cited estimate in the form actually used, and
   230	the calculation where a term or hypothesis appears or disappears.  When a
   231	displayed equation is identified by a source label, the label should appear on
   232	the right of the display, while the surrounding prose refers to the mathematical
   233	assertion itself.  The standard \texttt{amsmath} command \verb|\tag| is the
   234	right mechanism for this; a separate local convention should be introduced only
   235	if the standard mechanism is genuinely insufficient.  For a multi-line aligned
   236	display, tag the individual lines that carry the source information rather than
   237	forcing a long combined label below the equations.  Short
   238	scalar definitions and elementary inequalities should remain inline when the
   239	sentence reads better that way.  As in ordinary mathematical writing, a displayed
   240	formula is part of the surrounding sentence and should be punctuated accordingly.
   241	
   242	Bibliographic entries used only by these notes should live in
   243	\path{docs/paper-gaps/references.bib}.  A new note should ordinarily begin from
   244	\path{docs/paper-gaps/template.tex}, which records the common LaTeX preamble,
   245	the local bibliography, and a model for right-hand source labels in displayed
   246	equations.
   247	
   248	Blueprint prose cites a note like any other source, with
   249	\verb|\cite{gap:<slug>}|; the bibliography entry in
   250	\path{blueprint/src/references.bib} carries the published URL of the note,
   251	whether the note lives in this repository or in another one.  Lean docstrings
   252	and comments use the repository path form \path{docs/paper-gaps/<slug>.tex}.
   253	
   254	The note should then compare the cited source with the informal blueprint, if
   255	there is one, and with the formal statement.  This comparison should be written
   256	in ordinary mathematical prose.  Formal declaration names and source paths should
   257	be supplied only to identify the exact formal statements, and normally belong in
   258	footnotes.
   259	
   260	The conclusion should give a verdict.  It may say that there is no discrepancy,
   261	that the matter is only notational, that an intermediate estimate needs a
   262	harmless correction, that a hypothesis is missing, that there is a theorem-level
   263	gap, or that the question remains open.  The classification should reflect the
   264	mathematics, not the amount of formal work required.
   265	
   266	\section{Decision Principle}
   267	
   268	The formal development should not silently replace the cited assertion by a
   269	different one.  If the formal statement differs from the cited source, the
   270	reason for the difference should be written down.  Conversely, the note should
   271	not overstate the conclusion.  A wrong intermediate scalar is not a fatal gap in
   272	the theorem if the corrected scalar is bounded by the error parameter appearing
   273	in the theorem statement.
   274

1	# Blueprint Style Guide & Lessons Learned
     2	
     3	## Core Philosophy
     4	The blueprint is a **bridge between the mathematics and the Lean formalization**. A reader should be able to read a blueprint entry and immediately understand the corresponding Lean declaration. Conversely, someone reading the Lean code should find the blueprint proof sketch faithful to what the code actually does.
     5	
     6	## General Principles
     7	1. **Blueprint ↔ Lean must match.** Every `\lean{X}` tag must correspond to an actual Lean declaration. Every proof sketch must match what the Lean proof actually does — not a hand-wavy version of it.
     8	2. **Standalone.** `blueprint/` and any slides are independent — no cross-references, no shared files. Each has its own macros, its own `references.bib`.
     9	3. **Mathematical language only — zero Lean jargon.** No Lean identifiers in prose (no `selfImprovement_step`, no `PastingLemma.aux`, no `rintro ⟨X, hX⟩`). The `\lean{...}` tag is the link; the body text is standard mathematics. If you can't say it in math, rewrite it.
    10	4. **No filler prose.** Only precise definitions, theorem statements, and proof sketches. No "this is important because..." or "the self-improvement step governs the induction...".
    11	5. **Cite non-trivial things.** Basic definitions don't need citations. Important results and non-obvious definitions should cite the source paper.
    12	6. **Don't invent terminology or notation.** Don't create ad-hoc notation when standard notation exists. Don't name things that the literature doesn't name.
    13	7. **Match Lean's theorem/lemma/def exactly.** If Lean says `theorem X`, use `\begin{theorem}`. If Lean says `lemma X`, use `\begin{lemma}`. `\begin{proposition}` is allowed in blueprint prose when it improves mathematical readability, but still map it to an actual Lean `theorem`/`lemma` declaration via `\lean{...}`. Label prefix: `thm:` for theorem, `lem:` for lemma, `def:` for definition, `prop:` for proposition.
    14	
    15	### Remark On Mathematical Prose
    16	
    17	Blueprint entries should read as mathematical exposition, not as progress
    18	reports. The mathematical argument should determine the order of the prose:
    19	introduce the notation, state the assertion, give the proof or calculation, and
    20	then record Lean references through the usual blueprint tags. Lean declarations,
    21	file paths, and proof-status information should not become the visible structure
    22	of the paragraph. When referring to a source article, cite it bibliographically
    23	rather than relying on an uncited reference to the article.
    24	
    25	Use displayed formulae when the formula benefits from visual separation, and
    26	keep short scalar definitions or elementary inequalities inline when the
    27	sentence reads better that way. As in ordinary mathematical writing, displayed
    28	formulae should be punctuated as part of the sentences in which they occur.
    29	
    30	## Proof Sketches Must Match Lean
    31	This is the most important rule. Every proof in the blueprint must faithfully describe what the Lean proof does:
    32	
    33	- **Reference the actual lemmas used.** If the Lean proof calls `LDT.selfImprovement`, the blueprint proof should say "By Lemma X.Y (self-improvement)..." and list it in `\uses`.
    34	- **Do not use `\cref` or `\Cref`.** The blueprint does not load `cleveref`.
    35	  Spell out the kind of object and use ordinary references, for example
    36	  `Lemma~\ref{lem:self-improvement}` or `Theorem~\ref{thm:main-formal}`.
    37	- **Describe the actual proof structure.** If Lean does induction on a parameter, say so. If Lean uses a specific decomposition, name it.
    38	- **Don't hand-wave where Lean is specific.** "Standard argument" is not acceptable if Lean uses three specific lemmas. Name them.
    39	- **Don't be more specific than Lean.** If Lean uses `simp` to close a goal, a one-line sketch is fine.
    40	- **`\uses` in proofs must be accurate.** Only list what the proof actually uses, not what the statement mentions.
    41	
    42	## Source-Labelled Statements And Conditional Helpers
    43	
    44	If a blueprint theorem, lemma, or proposition carries a source label from the
    45	paper, the linked Lean declaration must state the same theorem, up to faithful
    46	formal encoding of the paper's domain.  Do not use `\lean{...}` and `\leanok`
    47	on the source-labelled statement to point to a conditional helper whose
    48	additional assumptions supply an unproved part of the paper proof.
    49	Changing the Lean statement away from `references/ldt-paper/` is strongly
    50	discouraged unless faithful formal encoding or a documented mathematical
    51	necessity requires it; the blueprint should make any such necessity explicit.
    52	
    53	Boundary hypotheses such as nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
    54	positivity of parameters, and denominator nonvanishing may be faithful when
    55	they express the mathematical domain that the paper leaves implicit.  By
    56	contrast, bridge inputs, residual data, repair hypotheses, producer
    57	assumptions, proof-obligation inputs, or package assumptions are proof debt.
    58	They must not be added to a source-labelled theorem statement.  If such data is
    59	still unproved, the source-labelled Lean theorem should keep the source-shaped
    60	statement and carry a tracked `sorry`, or the missing assertion should appear
    61	as the lowest named internal obligation with a tracked `sorry`.  A separately
    62	named conditional helper should not be introduced as a repair pattern.  If one
    63	already contains substantial proof content, it may remain temporarily only as
    64	quarantine: it needs a paper source, a tracking issue, and a discharge or
    65	deletion plan.  The blueprint should leave the paper theorem unmarked as
    66	proof-complete until the source-faithful Lean statement has a source-faithful
    67	proof.
    68	
    69	If a Lean theorem proves only a restricted version of a source theorem, the
    70	blueprint entry carrying `\leanok` must state that restriction in the theorem
    71	statement itself.  It must not be cited as the unrestricted source theorem.
    72	When the only Lean declaration available for a source label has extra
    73	non-paper assumptions, remove the `\leanok` claim from the source-labelled
    74	entry or move the restricted statement to a separate Lean-only entry.  The
    75	unrestricted paper theorem remains unformalized until a Lean statement with
    76	the source's hypothesis set exists.
    77	
    78	## Notation Consistency
    79	Notation must be **internally consistent** across the entire blueprint and **close to what the Lean code expresses**:
    80	
    81	- **Indices**: 0-indexed where matching `Fin n` in Lean
    82	- **Finite fields / alphabets**: use standard notation for the alphabet $\Sigma$ and finite fields $\mathbb{F}_q$
    83	- **Measurements**: use standard quantum measurement notation (projective measurements, POVMs)
    84	- **Strategies**: quantum strategies for nonlocal games should use standard notation from the literature
    85	- **Expansion**: use standard notation for graph expansion parameters
    86	- **Macros** (in `macros/common.tex`): define project-specific macros and use them consistently
    87	
    88	The original reference controls notation whenever it gives a usable convention.
    89	If the blueprint needs a different symbol, index convention, or name in order to
    90	match Lean, introduce it explicitly and relate it to the paper notation in the
    91	same paragraph.  Do not let a `\lean{...}` tag, a Lean namespace, or a file name
    92	be the only explanation of a changed term.
    93	
    94	When a public Lean declaration is a formalization-only auxiliary lemma, the
    95	blueprint should say so before listing the declaration.  The surrounding prose
    96	should identify the paper theorem, equation, or construction that the auxiliary
    97	lemma supports, and should avoid making the auxiliary name look like a named
    98	result from the source article.
    99	
   100	## What NOT to Put in the Blueprint
   101	- **Lean identifier names in math text.** Write "the self-improvement lemma", never "the `selfImprovement` step". The `\lean{LDT.selfImprovement}` tag handles the linking.
   102	- **Implementation details.** Don't say "bundled as an element of the Euclidean space" or "using `EuclideanSpace.equiv`". Describe the mathematical object.
   103	- **Ad-hoc notation.** Don't invent superscripts or subscripts to distinguish from existing notation. Use standard conventions.
   104	- **Function-call syntax.** Use mathematical notation, not programming notation.
   105	- **Redundant definitions.** If two blueprint definitions describe the same mathematical object, consolidate them. Each definition should introduce genuinely new mathematical content.
   106	- **Lean namespace prefixes in prose.** Don't write "the `LDT.PastingLemma`" — write "the pasting lemma".
   107	
   108	## Banned AI/Software Language (enforced in both blueprint AND Lean code)
   109	The blueprint reads as a **mathematical document**, not software documentation. The following patterns are banned in ALL reader-facing text (section titles, theorem names, proof sketches, remarks, chapter preambles) and in ALL Lean docstrings, comments, and section names:
   110	
   111	### Banned terms → replacements:
   112	| Banned | Use instead |
   113	|--------|------------|
   114	| "Assembly" (as section/chapter title) | "Proof of [theorem]", "Construction", "Composition" |
   115	| "Pipeline" | "reduction", "construction", "proof chain" |
   116	| "Bridge" (as noun for a connection) | "connection", name by mathematical content |
   117	| "Handoff" / "hand off" | "transition", "continuation", or drop entirely |
   118	| "In this blueprint" / "Within this blueprint" | "here", "in what follows", or omit |
   119	| "Honest" (as adjective for rigorous) | "exact", "faithful", "unconditional", "complete" |
   120	| "Glue layer" | "intermediate construction", "connecting results" |
   121	| "Re-export" / "reexport" | "provides", "re-states" |
   122	| "Wiring" / "wire up" | "connecting", "composing", "combining" |
   123	| "Package" (as noun for a data bundle) | "form", "data", "structure" |
   124	| "Sorry-free" | acceptable only in Lean-specific technical context |
   125	
   126	### Additional rules:
   127	- **Section names in Lean**: use mathematical terms (`section QuantumSoundness`, `section SelfImprovement`, `section PastingLemma`), not organizational terms (`section Assembly`, `section Pipeline`).
   128	- **Internal LaTeX labels** (e.g., `\label{ch:soundness}`) are not reader-facing and need not be renamed if doing so would break cross-references. But NEW labels should follow the standard.
   129	- **Definitions that are actually theorems**: if a statement asserts a mathematical fact, it must be `\begin{theorem}`, not `\begin{definition}`. Definitions introduce new objects; theorems prove properties.
   130	
   131	## `\uses` Dependency Guidelines
   132	- **Statement `\uses`**: list only what's needed to *state* the result (typically definitions of the objects involved). Keep minimal — transitive deps are automatic.
   133	- **Proof `\uses`**: list only what the proof *actually calls*. Don't list definitions unless the proof unfolds that definition.
   134	- **Never self-reference**: a proof's `\uses` must NOT include the label of the theorem it proves.
   135	
   136	## Recording Formalization-Only Lemmas
   137	Some Lean lemmas are genuine proof infrastructure rather than named statements
   138	from the original papers. These must be traceable without making the blueprint
   139	look as if the paper stated them.
   140	
   141	- If a declaration directly formalizes a paper or blueprint statement, record
   142	  it as usual with `\lean{...}` on that statement and cite the relevant source.
   143	- If a public declaration is an auxiliary lemma introduced only for the Lean
   144	  proof, make that status explicit. Its Lean docstring should say that it is a
   145	  formalization-only auxiliary lemma and should name the nearby paper equation,
   146	  line range, or blueprint result it supports.
   147	- If such an auxiliary declaration is important enough to be referenced from
   148	  the blueprint, give it a clearly subordinate blueprint node, for example
   149	  `[Formalization support for ...]`, and state in the first sentence that the
   150	  lemma is not a named statement of the paper but isolates a step used in the
   151	  Lean proof.
   152	- Connect auxiliary nodes to the corresponding result from the paper with `\uses{...}` from
   153	  the proof that actually calls them. Do not add them only to silence a sync
   154	  warning; the dependency edge should explain where the auxiliary result is
   155	  used.
   156	- Do not mark an auxiliary node with proof-level `\leanok` unless its Lean proof
   157	  is complete and `#print axioms` has no `sorryAx`. Statement-level `\leanok`
   158	  is acceptable only when the Lean statement is intentionally recorded but the
   159	  proof remains tracked as incomplete.
   160	
   161	## Blueprint Structure
   162	- `content.tex` is a router: `\input{chapter/ch01_intro}` etc.
   163	- Each chapter is a separate file in `chapter/`
   164	- Definitions/theorems numbered within chapters: `\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}[chapter]`
   165	
   166	## Lean Blueprint Macros
   167	- `\lean{Namespace.DeclName}` — links to Lean declaration
   168	- `\leanok` — context-sensitive marker; see "Statement-level vs proof-level `\leanok`" below
   169	- `\uses{label1, label2}` — declares dependency edges for the graph
   170	- `\notready` — marks as not ready for formalization (orange in graph)
   171	- `\mathlibok` — already in Mathlib (dark green in graph; see legend note below)
   172	
   173	### Statement-level vs proof-level `\leanok`
   174	
   175	`\leanok` is context-sensitive for human review and graph interpretation. The same macro is used for two different claims, so reviewers should read it by placement rather than by raw token count.
   176	
   177	**Statement-level `\leanok`.** Place this inside a `theorem`, `lemma`, `proposition`, `corollary`, or `definition` environment, on its own line immediately after `\lean{...}`. It says that the corresponding Lean declaration exists and that its statement matches the blueprint or paper statement. It does **not** say that the Lean proof already exists or is complete. For definitions, this is the only `\leanok` marker.
   178	
   179	**Proof-level `\leanok`.** Place this inside the matching `proof` environment, preferably as the first line after `\begin{proof}`. The canonical current placement is the theorem `thm:commutativity-points` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch08_commutativity.tex:8-19`, where the statement block has `\leanok` immediately after `\lean{...}` and the proof block begins with another `\leanok`. This marker says that the Lean proof is complete and free of unresolved `sorry` or unjustified project-level `axiom` shortcuts. In particular, `#print axioms <decl>` must show no `sorryAx`, and the declaration must satisfy the broader blocker rules in the lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference and [`docs/project_conventions.md`](project_conventions.md).
   180	
   181	A theorem, lemma, proposition, or corollary node is **fully formalized in Lean if and only if it has both markers**: statement-level `\leanok` in the statement block and proof-level `\leanok` in the proof block. Statement-level without proof-level means “the statement has been transcribed and matched, but the proof is not yet certified complete.” Definitions have no proof block, so statement-level `\leanok` alone is enough there.
   182	
   183	Excerpt from `blueprint/src/chapter/ch08_commutativity.tex:8-19`:
   184	
   185	```latex
   186	\begin{theorem}[Commutativity of the point measurements]\label{thm:commutativity-points}
   187	  \lean{MIPStarRE.LDT.CommutativityPoints.commutativityPoints}
   188	  \leanok
   189	  \uses{def:good-strategy, def:approx_delta}
   190	  Let $(\psi,A,B,L)$ be an $(\eps,\delta,\gamma)$-good symmetric strategy.
   191	\end{theorem}
   192	\begin{proof}
   193	  \leanok
   194	  The strategy passes the diagonal lines test with probability $1-\gamma$.
   195	\end{proof}
   196	```
   197	
   198	**Current CI behavior.** The advisory Blueprint ↔ Lean sync check in [`docs/ci-blueprint-sync.md`](ci-blueprint-sync.md) distinguishes the two placements. Only proof-level `\leanok` whose axiom closure contains `sorryAx` (or whose harness output cannot be parsed) is reported as an **error**. Statement-level-only `\leanok` with the same finding is downgraded to a **warning**, because statement-level does not claim proof completeness. Each audit line is annotated with the observed placement so reviewers can tell statement-sync work apart from proof-completion work.
   199	
   200	`leanblueprint` does not use distinct macro names for these two claims, so audits must distinguish them by environment context rather than by raw `\leanok` counts. A future split such as `\leanokstmt` / `\leanokproof` could make that distinction explicit, but that is only a possible later cleanup; the current convention is to keep `\leanok` and rely on placement.
   201	
   202	A recurring historical example is the chapter 4 `Q/X/\widehat X/P` witness
   203	layer.  Once Lean has construction theorems deriving the displayed identities
   204	and estimates from the rank-reduction, sigma-range, positive-Gram, native
   205	spectral-theorem, or rectangular-SVD hypotheses, the corresponding blueprint
   206	entries may carry `\leanok`.  A declaration that merely projects an identity
   207	from an opaque data record is not enough by itself, and a theorem depending on
   208	extra rectangular-SVD data should not be used as evidence for an unconditional
   209	paper statement unless a separate construction supplies that data.
   210	
   211	## Dependency Graph Colors (web)
   212	- **Light green box**: definition with `\lean` + `\leanok` (defined in Lean)
   213	- **Green**: theorem/lemma/proposition/corollary with `\lean` + statement-level `\leanok` (statement matched in Lean)
   214	- **Dark green**: either (i) theorem/lemma/proposition/corollary with both statement-level and proof-level `\leanok` (fully formalized in Lean), or (ii) a `\mathlibok` node
   215	- **Blue**: ready to state/prove (all deps are done)
   216	- **Orange**: `\notready` (needs more blueprint work)
   217	
   218	## Bibliography Workflow
   219	1. Edit `blueprint/src/references.bib` (standalone, AuthorYYYYKeyword keys)
   220	2. Run `texra-blueprint bbl` from the repository root — it regenerates
   221	   `blueprint/src/web.bbl` from the `\cite` keys in the blueprint sources.
   222	   `web.bbl` is not committed (`.gitignore` covers `*.bbl`); every CI job
   223	   that runs the web build regenerates it first, and so must a local run.
   224	3. Run `leanblueprint web` (plasTeX reads `web.bbl`)
   225	4. The PDF build needs no separate step: `leanblueprint pdf` runs bibtex on
   226	   `print.tex` itself, and `print.bbl` never feeds the web build.
   227	5. Citation key format: e.g., `Ji2020MIPStar`, `Natarajan2020Quantum`
   228	6. Paper-gap notes: blueprint prose cites `\cite{gap:<slug>}` (never the raw
   229	   `docs/paper-gaps/<slug>.tex` path); each cited note has a `@techreport`
   230	   entry in `blueprint/src/references.bib` with `type = {Paper-gap note}`,
   231	   whose `note` field carries the published PDF URL as `\url{...}` (the
   232	   alpha style of the PDF build drops `url` fields for techreport entries).
   233	   `texra-blueprint bbl` renders such entries with slug-shaped citation
   234	   labels (e.g. `[issue-906-main-formal-k-bound]`) in the web bibliography,
   235	   while ordinary entries keep alpha labels. Lean docstrings and comments
   236	   keep the repository path form.
   237	
   238	## Stale/Corrupt Aux File Recovery
   239	If LaTeX reports `! File ended while scanning use of \@newl@bel` on startup:
   240	- The `.aux` file was truncated by a previous killed/timed-out run
   241	- Fix: `rm -f blueprint/src/print.aux blueprint/print/print.aux blueprint/print.aux`
   242	- Then rerun latexmk — it rebuilds the aux from scratch cleanly
   243	- `web.bbl` is unaffected: it comes from `texra-blueprint bbl`, not from
   244	  `print.bbl`
   245	
   246	## Build Commands
   247	```bash
   248	leanblueprint pdf     # PDF → blueprint/print/print.pdf
   249	leanblueprint web     # HTML → blueprint/web/
   250	leanblueprint serve   # local server at http://0.0.0.0:8000/
   251	leanblueprint all     # pdf + web + checkdecls
   252	```

1	# Mathematical Language Guidelines
     2	
     3	MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
     4	the formalization with the paper and blueprint.
     5	
     6	This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
     7	naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
     8	`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.
     9	
    10	## Scope
    11	
    12	These guidelines apply to:
    13	
    14	- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
    15	- module docstrings;
    16	- declaration docstrings;
    17	- documentation-visible section comments;
    18	- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
    19	- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
    20	- issue titles and issue bodies;
    21	- PR titles and PR descriptions.
    22	
    23	## Source of Truth
    24	
    25	Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:
    26	
    27	1. `references/ldt-paper/`
    28	2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
    29	3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files
    30	
    31	When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
    32	example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
    33	projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.
    34	
    35	## Reference Notation And Terminology
    36	
    37	The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
    38	reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
    39	docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
    40	without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.
    41	
    42	When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
    43	location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
    44	first applicable location in the following order:
    45	
    46	1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
    47	   differs from the paper;
    48	2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
    49	   family of declarations in that file;
    50	3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
    51	   blueprint;
    52	4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
    53	   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.
    54	
    55	The explanation should say:
    56	
    57	- the notation or term used in the paper;
    58	- the Lean object or name which represents it;
    59	- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
    60	- the scope in which the replacement should be used.
    61	
    62	A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
    63	where future readers can learn it.
    64	
    65	Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
    66	should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
    67	rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.
    68	
    69	## Naming Norm
    70	
    71	Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
    72	conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
    73	assembled.
    74	
    75	Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
    76	`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
    77	uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
    78	such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
    79	clearer phrase.
    80	
    81	This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
    82	Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
    83	blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
    84	mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
    85	number, or implementation history.
    86	
    87	### Concrete examples
    88	
    89	The table below illustrates the naming norm with examples patterned on the
    90	codebase and on names seen during review.  Some entries are existing names;
    91	others are proposed names for future refactors.  The "avoid" column lists
    92	process-shaped names that encode the history of how the formalization was
    93	assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
    94	paper or blueprint would recognize.
    95	
    96	| Avoid (process-shaped)                        | Prefer (mathematical)                     | Rationale                                              |
    97	|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
    98	| `Line130`                                     | `ProjectiveConsistency`                   | Paper Lemma 5.13, not "the line-130 identity"          |
    99	| `Line169`                                     | `CompletionTransport`                     | Paper Lemma 5.16, step that transports completed data  |
   100	| `Step6`                                       | `Orthonormalization`                      | Paper Section 5, the orthonormalization construction   |
   101	| `FinalAssembly`                               | `DiagonalCompletion`                      | Paper Lemma 5.17, constructing a diagonal POVM         |
   102	| `OneShotIneq`                                 | `SelfConsistencyDataProcessing` (or existing module `Preliminaries.SelfConsistency.DataProcessing`)           | Paper's data-processing inequality for self-consistency |
   103	| `PipelineCheck`                               | `ErrorPropagationBound` (proposed)                   | The bound that propagates error through the test       |
   104	| `QxpLayerWrapper`                             | `ProjectivePOVMCompletion` (proposed)                | The construction from round-projectors to POVMs        |
   105	| `RawSpectralTruncation`                       | `SpectralTruncation`                      | The paper's spectral truncation, not an "unwrapped" version |
   106	| `AddInUStep3To5`                              | `AddInUUpperExcessMass` (proposed)                  | Paper Addendum in §U, the upper excess-mass estimate   |
   107	| `AddInUStep12`                                | `AddInUCommutationTail` (proposed)                   | Paper Addendum in §U, the commutation tail estimate    |
   108	
   109	An avoided name is acceptable only when the cited paper itself uses that
   110	phrase as the mathematical name (e.g., a lemma the paper calls "Step 2").
   111	In that case the docstring should cite the paper's phrasing.
   112	
   113	File-split PRs are a common place where this rule matters: new leaves should be
   114	named by the mathematical boundary they isolate, and any public declarations
   115	exposed by the split should be reviewed under the same standard.
   116	
   117	### Shared helpers
   118	
   119	When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
   120	more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
   121	shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
   122	ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
   123	call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.
   124	
   125	Procedure:
   126	
   127	1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   128	   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   129	   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   130	   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   131	   explicit argument.
   132	2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   133	   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   134	   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   135	   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   136	   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
   137	3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   138	   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
   139	4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   140	   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   141	   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   142	   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   143	   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   144	   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
   145	5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   146	   blueprint location it supports.
   147	
   148	### Legacy identifier treatment
   149	
   150	If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
   151	describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
   152	identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
   153	in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.
   154	
   155	Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
   156	public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
   157	shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
   158	blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.
   159	
   160	## Review Checklist
   161	
   162	Reviewers should use this checklist when examining public names and
   163	documentation prose.  Flag any item that fails.
   164	
   165	- [ ] **Naming.**  Do public declaration names, namespace names, module names,
   166	      theorem field names, and docstring prose describe a mathematical object,
   167	      hypothesis, or conclusion?  Or do they encode the history of how the
   168	      formalization was assembled (paper line numbers, workflow steps,
   169	      implementation-phase labels)?
   170	- [ ] **Source alignment.**  For the mathematical content under review, does
   171	      the prose use the terminology in `references/ldt-paper/` or the
   172	      blueprint?  Are process words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`,
   173	      `raw`, `oneShot`, or `liveBlock` used as mathematical terms when the
   174	      source does not use them that way?
   175	- [ ] **Deviation documented.**  If a Lean name or representation differs from
   176	      the paper, is the deviation documented in a declaration docstring,
   177	      module docstring, blueprint paragraph, or `docs/paper-gaps/` note, in
   178	      that order of preference?
   179	- [ ] **Auxiliary lemmas.**  Are formalization-only auxiliary lemmas introduced
   180	      as such, with prose naming the nearby paper equation, theorem, or
   181	      construction they support?
   182	- [ ] **Shared helpers.**  Does the PR introduce a helper that already exists
   183	      (or near-exists) in another chapter-local leaf?  If so, has it been
   184	      consolidated into a common module with a mathematical name?
   185	- [ ] **Legacy IDs.**  If a legacy Lean identifier is mentioned, is the
   186	      mathematical object described in paper terminology?  If an old public
   187	      identifier cannot be renamed yet, is the required migration recorded in
   188	      the issue, PR description, or an audit file?
   189	- [ ] **Pass-through names.**  Does the PR add an empty pass-through
   190	      abbreviation that introduces a second public name without adding
   191	      mathematical content?  Reject it unless it is a documented compatibility
   192	      wrapper preserving paper-facing or blueprint-facing terminology.
   193	
   194	Review-fix PRs touching a surface covered by an active audit should read the
   195	relevant audit before changing names or prose.

  1790		\Id_{\alice \alice' \alice''} \otimes M^{(\Point,W),u}_a &\simeq_\eps  M^{(\Point,W),u}_a \otimes \Id_{\bob \bob' \bob''}\;,
  1791		\end{align}
  1792		where $M^{(\Pauli,W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} = \sum_{h : g_h(u) = a} M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h$. 
  1793	From \Cref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis} we get that
  1794		\begin{equation}
  1795		\label{eq:qld-unitary-4}
  1796			M^{(\Point,W),u}_a \otimes \Id_{\bob \bob' \bob''} \simeq_{\delta_S} \Id_{\alice \alice' \alice''}  \otimes \tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a\;.
  1797		\end{equation}
  1798	Using \Cref{fact:triangle-for-simeq} with Equations \eqref{eq:qld-unitary-2}, \eqref{eq:qld-unitary-3}, and \eqref{eq:qld-unitary-4}, we get 
  1799		\begin{equation}
  1800			\label{eq:qld-unitary-5}
  1801			M^{(\Pauli,W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} \otimes \Id_{\bob \bob' \bob''} \simeq_{\sqrt{\delta_S}} \Id_{\alice \alice' \alice''}  \otimes \tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a\;,
  1802		\end{equation}
  1803		where we used that $\delta_S \geq \eps$. 
  1804		
  1805		Next, we have for all $u \in \F_q^m$ 
  1806		\begin{align}
  1807			&V_\bob \, \tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a \, V_\bob^\dagger \notag \\
  1808			= &\sum_{g_X, g_Z} \Big( \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}  \Big)_{\bob \bob'} \otimes \Big ( \tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^W_{g_W(u) - a}(\ind_m(u))    \tau^Z(\coded(g_X))^\dagger \tau^X(\coded(g_Z))^\dagger \Big)_{\bob ''} \notag \\
  1809			= &\sum_{g_X, g_Z} \Big( \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}  \Big)_{\bob \bob'} \otimes \sum_{h : g_h(u) = g_W(u) - a} \Big ( \tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^W_h   \tau^Z(\coded(g_X))^\dagger \tau^X(\coded(g_Z))^\dagger \Big)_{\bob ''} \notag \\
  1810			= &\sum_{g_X, g_Z} \Big( \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}  \Big)_{\bob \bob'} \otimes \sum_{h : g_h(u) = g_W(u) - a} \Big ( \tau^W_{h + \coded(g_W)}   \Big)_{\bob ''} \notag \\
  1811		= &\sum_{g_X, g_Z} \Big( \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}  \Big)_{\bob \bob'} \otimes \sum_{h : g_h(u) = a} \Big ( \tau^W_{h}   \Big)_{\bob ''} \notag \\
  1812	= &\Id_{\bob \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_{[g_h(u)=a]})_{\bob''}\;,		\label{eq:qld-unitary-6}
  1813		\end{align}
  1814		where in the second line we expanded out the definitions of $V_\bob$ and $\tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a$ (defined in \cref{eq:tilde_M}); in the third line we expanded out the definition of $\tau^W_{g_W(u) - a}(\ind_m(u))$ (defined in \cref{eq:def-tauwu}) and used the fact that for all $h \in \F_q^M$, the inner product $h \cdot \ind_m(u)$ is equal to $g_h(u)$; in the fourth line we used the identities
  1815		\[
  1816			\tau^X(s) \tau^Z_h \tau^X(s)^\dagger = \tau^Z_{h + s} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \tau^Z(s) \tau^X_h \tau^Z(s)^\dagger = \tau^X_{h + s}~;
  1817		\]
  1818		and in the fifth line is due to the following short calculation: for all fixed $g_W$ we have
  1819		\begin{align*}
  1820			\sum_{h : g_h(u) = g_W(u) - a}  \tau^W_{h + \coded(g_W)} = \sum_{h: g_W(u) - g_h(u) = a} \tau^W_{h + \coded(g_W)} = \sum_{h: g_W(u) + g_h(u) = a} \tau^W_{h + \coded(g_W)} = \sum_{h': g_{h'}(u) = a} \tau^W_{h'}~.
  1821		\end{align*}

  1823		
  1824		
  1825	
  1826	
  1827	Let $\ket{\Delta} = \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$. We show that $V_\alice \, \Big(M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \Big)_{\alice} \, V_\alice^\dagger \approx_{\delta_\qld} \Id_{\alice \alice'} \otimes (\tau^W_h)_{\alice''}$ (the argument for the operators acting on registers $\bob \bob' \bob''$ proceeds identically). 
  1828		\begin{align}
  1829			&\sum_h \bra{\Delta} \left ( V_\alice \, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \, V_\alice^\dagger - (\tau^W_h)_{\alice''}  \right)^\dagger \left ( V_\alice \, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \, V_\alice^\dagger - (\tau^W_h)_{\alice''} \right) \ket{\Delta} \notag \\
  1830			&= 2 - 2 \Re \, \sum_h \bra{\Delta} V_\alice\, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \, V_\alice^\dagger  \, (\tau^W_h)_{\alice''} \ket{\Delta} \notag \\
  1831			&= 2 - 2 \, \sum_h \bra{\Delta} V_\alice \, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \, V_\alice^\dagger  \, \otimes (\tau^W_h)_{\bob''} \ket{\Delta} \label{eq:qld-unitary-7}
  1832	\end{align}
  1833		where in the last line we used that $(\tau^W_h)_{\alice''} \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits} = (\tau^W_h)_{\bob''} \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$.
  1834		We now claim that
  1835		\begin{align}
  1836		&  \, \sum_h \bra{\Delta} V_\alice \, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \, V_\alice^\dagger  \, \otimes (\tau^W_h)_{\bob''} \ket{\Delta}  \notag \\
  1837		&\approx_{md/q}  \E_u \sum_{\substack{h, h' : \\ g_h(u) = g_{h'}(u)}} \bra{\Delta} V_\alice \, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \, V_\alice^\dagger  \, \otimes (\tau^W_{h'})_{\bob''} \ket{\Delta} \label{eq:qld-unitary-8} \\
  1838		&=  \E_u \sum_{a \in \F_q} \bra{\Delta} V_\alice \, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} \, V_\alice^\dagger \, \otimes (\tau^W_{[g_h(u)=a]})_{\bob''} \ket{\Delta} \notag \\
  1839		&=  \E_u \sum_{a \in \F_q} \bra{\Delta} V_\alice \, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} \, V_\alice^\dagger \, \otimes V_\bob  \, \tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a \, V_\bob^\dagger \ket{\Delta} \label{eq:qld-unitary-9}

  1843			& \E_u \sum_{\substack{h \neq h' : \\ g_h(u) = g_{h'}(u)}} \bra{\Delta} V_\alice \, M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \, V_\alice^\dagger  \, \otimes (\tau^W_{h'})_{\bob''} \ket{\Delta}  \\

  1857		\text{\cref{eq:qld-unitary-7}} \leq O(\delta_S^{1/4} + md/q)\;.

  1862	We now prove \Cref{thm:pauli-appendix}. 
  1863	\begin{proof}[Proof of \Cref{thm:pauli-appendix}]
  1864		Let $\strategy = (\psi,M)$ be a projective strategy for $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeeds with probability at least $1 - \eps$, where $\ket{\psi}$ is a bipartite state on registers $\alice \bob$. As mentioned at the beginning of \Cref{sec:commutation}, we assume that the state $\ket{\psi}$ is padded with sufficiently many ancilla $\ket{0}$ qubits. Let $\phi_\alice$ be the following isometry mapping the register $\alice$ to the registers $\alice \alice' \alice''$ where $\alice'$ and $\alice''$ are isomorphic to $(\C^q)^{\otimes \nqubits}$:
  1865		\[
  1866			\phi_\alice: \ket{\theta}_\alice \mapsto V_\alice (\ket{\theta}_\alice \otimes (\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits})_{\alice' \alice''})
  1867		\]
  1868		where $V_\alice$ is the unitary acting on $\alice \alice' \alice''$ from \Cref{lem:qld-unitary}. Define the isometry $\phi_\bob$ analogously. \Cref{lem:qld-unitary} then implies that there exists a state $\ket{\aux}$ on registers $\alice \alice' \bob \bob'$ such that
  1869		\[
  1870			\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_\bob \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits} \right \|^2 \leq \delta_\qld
  1871		\]
  1872		and for $W \in \{X,Z\}$,
  1873		\[
  1874			\phi_\alice \, (M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h)_\alice \, \phi_\alice^\dagger \approx_{\delta_\qld} (\tau^W_h)_{\alice''} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \phi_\bob \, (M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h)_\bob \, \phi_\bob^\dagger \approx_{\delta_\qld} (\tau^W_h)_{\bob''}
  1875		\]
  1876		where the $\approx$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$. This shows that $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ is a self-test for the strategy $\strategy^\pauli$ with robustness $\delta_\qld(\eps,m,d,q)$. We conclude the proof by making the identification of registers $\alice \alice'$ with $\alice'$ and $\bob \bob'$ with $\bob'$ to be consistent with the statement of \Cref{thm:pauli-appendix}. We also note that, when unpacking the dependence on parameters $\eps, m, d, q$, the function $\delta_\qld(\eps,m,d,q) = O(\delta_S^{1/4} + md/q)$ has the form $a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for some universal constants $a > 1, 0 < b < 1$, as desired.
  1877	\end{proof}

item.text: The source uses one enlarged error scale throughout the construction lemma and then one extraction scale in the swap lemma, but it does not expose numerical constants theorem-by-theorem. I’m mapping the Lean declarations now; the key question is whether their separate existential constants are merely a decomposition of the source’s single big-O witness or a genuine mismatch that should be repaired in Lean.

   347			\bigl\| \phi_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \phi_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\psi} - \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M} \bigr\|^2 \leq \delta_{\mathrm{qld}}\;.
   348		\]
   349		% Transfer step added: the source (lines 1864--1875 of
   350		% 14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex) passes directly from the
   351		% conjugation estimates of lem:qld-unitary, which concern the
   352		% unitarily conjugated operators V (M_h ot Id) V^dagger, to the
   353		% corresponding estimates for the isometry phi, whose conjugation
   354		% inserts the projection onto its range; the range-projection
   355		% argument below supplies the missing step.
   356		Item~2 of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-unitary} concerns the unitarily conjugated operators $N^W_h = V_{\mathrm{A}} \, (M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h)_{\mathrm{A}} \, V_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger$, whereas conjugation by the isometry $\phi_{\mathrm{A}}$ additionally inserts the projection $Q_{\mathrm{A}} = \phi_{\mathrm{A}} \phi_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger = V_{\mathrm{A}} \, \bigl(\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}\bra{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}\bigr)_{\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''} \, V_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger$ onto the range of $\phi_{\mathrm{A}}$: since $(M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h)_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\bigl(\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}\bra{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}\bigr)_{\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''}$ act on disjoint registers and hence commute,
   357		\[
   358			\phi_{\mathrm{A}} \, (M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h)_{\mathrm{A}} \, \phi_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger
   359			= V_{\mathrm{A}} \, \Bigl( (M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h)_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \bigl(\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}\bra{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}\bigr)_{\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''} \Bigr) \, V_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger
   360			= N^W_h \, Q_{\mathrm{A}} = Q_{\mathrm{A}} \, N^W_h\;.
   361		\]
   362		The estimates transfer from $N^W_h$ to $\phi_{\mathrm{A}} \, (M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h)_{\mathrm{A}} \, \phi_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger$ as follows. Write $\ket{\Delta} = \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$ and $\ket{\vartheta} = \phi_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \phi_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\psi}$. Since $\phi_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger \phi_{\mathrm{A}} = \Id$, the projection $\Id - Q_{\mathrm{A}}$ annihilates $\ket{\vartheta}$, so the displayed bound above gives
   363		\[
   364			\bigl\| (\Id - Q_{\mathrm{A}}) \ket{\Delta} \bigr\|^2
   365			= \bigl\| (\Id - Q_{\mathrm{A}}) (\ket{\Delta} - \ket{\vartheta}) \bigr\|^2
   366			\leq \bigl\| \ket{\Delta} - \ket{\vartheta} \bigr\|^2
   367			\leq \delta_{\mathrm{qld}}\;.
   368		\]
   369		Since the strategy is projective, the operators $N^W_h$, for $h \in \F_q^M$, are mutually orthogonal projectors summing to the identity, so $\sum_h \| N^W_h \ket{\xi} \|^2 = \| \ket{\xi} \|^2$ for every vector $\ket{\xi}$. Decomposing
   370		\[
   371			\bigl( \phi_{\mathrm{A}} \, (M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h)_{\mathrm{A}} \, \phi_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger - (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{A}''} \bigr) \ket{\Delta}
   372			= \bigl( N^W_h - (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{A}''} \bigr) \ket{\Delta} - N^W_h (\Id - Q_{\mathrm{A}}) \ket{\Delta}
   373		\]
   374		and summing the squared norms over $h$ via $\| \xi - \xi' \|^2 \leq 2\|\xi\|^2 + 2\|\xi'\|^2$, the first terms contribute $O(\delta_{\mathrm{qld}})$ by Item~2 of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-unitary} and the second terms contribute at most $2 \| (\Id - Q_{\mathrm{A}}) \ket{\Delta} \|^2 \leq 2\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}$; hence, for $W \in \{X,Z\}$,
   375		\[
   376			\phi_{\mathrm{A}} \, (M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h)_{\mathrm{A}} \, \phi_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger \approx_{\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}} (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{A}''}
   377			\qquad \text{and, by the identical argument,} \qquad
   378			\phi_{\mathrm{B}} \, (M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h)_{\mathrm{B}} \, \phi_{\mathrm{B}}^\dagger \approx_{\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}} (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{B}''}\;,
   379		\]
   380		where the $\approx$ statements hold with respect to the state $\ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$ and the answer summation is over $h \in \F_q^M$; the constant implicit in $\approx_{\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}}$ (Definition~\ref{def:povm-distance}) absorbs the factors accumulated above. This shows that the game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$ is a self-test, with robustness $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps,m,d,q)$, for the canonical Pauli strategy of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness}. Identifying the registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'$ with $\mathrm{A}'$ and $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'$ with $\mathrm{B}'$ matches the statement of Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}, in which $\phi_{\mathrm{A}}\colon \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{A}} \to \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{A}'} \ot \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{A}''}$. Finally, unpacking the dependence on the parameters $\eps, m, d, q$, the function $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps,m,d,q) = O(\delta_P^{1/4} + md/q)$ has the form $a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for universal constants $a > 1$ and $0 < b < 1$; here $\delta_P = C(\delta_G + \sqrt{\eps} + md/q)$ and $\delta_G$ already has that form. See Remark~\ref{rem:pauli-robustness-form} for the reconciliation with the statement of Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}.
   381	\end{proof}
   382	
   383	\begin{remark}[Norm conventions in the robustness bound]\label{rem:pauli-robustness-form}
   384		The proof above, following the source, establishes the first conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} in the squared form $\| \phi_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \phi_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\psi} - \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M} \|^2 \leq \delta_{\mathrm{qld}}$, whereas the theorem bounds the unsquared norm by $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps,m,d,q)$. The two are reconciled by replacing the exponent $b$ with $b/2$ and enlarging $a$, since the class of functions $a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ is closed under square roots up to such adjustments of the universal constants. Similarly, the closing sentence of the source proof asserts constants $a > 1$ and $0 < b < 1$, while Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} requires only $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$; the former implies the latter.
   385	\end{remark}

blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:28:	The source states the constructions of this chapter in terms of its boolean decoding map (the case $H = \{0,1\}$ of Definition~\ref{def:decoding-map}) while describing that map as returning the string of \emph{all} evaluations of $g$ on the hypercube. The proofs require the latter reading, $H = \F_q$, which is adopted throughout this chapter: the linearity of $\mathrm{Dec}$ and the identity $\mathrm{Dec}(g_h) = h$ for all $h \in \F_q^{M}$, both of which fail for the boolean map, are used in the symmetry step of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis} and in the conjugation identity \eqref{eq:qld-unitary-6}. The source further asserts the identity $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u) = g(u)$ for every $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$. Since the left-hand side equals $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)}(u)$, the identity, taken for all $u \in \F_q^m$, states that the multilinear representative $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)}$ and $g$ induce the same function on $\F_q^m$. Every encoding satisfies it, because then $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)} = g$ as polynomial representatives; a polynomial that is not an encoding need not: for $m = 1$, $d \geq 2$, and $q > 2$, the polynomial $g(x) = x^2$ has $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_1(u) = u$, which differs from $g(u) = u^2$ at every $u \notin \{0,1\}$. When $d \leq q-1$ the failure at some $u$ characterizes the polynomials that are not encodings, since evaluation is injective on representatives of individual degree at most $q-1$ (Definition~\ref{def:polynomials-degree}); when $d \geq q$ it does not: for the admissible tuple $(q,m,d) = (8,1,8)$, the polynomial $g(x) = x^8$ is not an encoding, yet $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_1(u) = u = u^8 = g(u)$ for every $u \in \F_8$. Accordingly, the proofs below invoke the identity only for encodings; in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis} the contribution of the remaining outcomes is controlled by the bound \eqref{eq:qld-nonencoding-mass} on the mass that the measurement of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7} places on polynomials that are not encodings, while in the conjugation identity \eqref{eq:qld-unitary-6} the quantity $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u)$ cancels exactly.

360		Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc} introduces the set $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ of
   361		polynomials in $\F_q[x_1, \dots, x_m]$ of degree at most $d$ in each
   362		variable, identified by their polynomial representatives rather than by the
   363		functions they induce. Evaluation maps $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ onto the set of
   364		$m$-variate polynomials of individual degree at most $\min(d, q-1)$ in the
   365		sense above; for $d \le q-1$ this map is a bijection, while for $d \ge q$
   366		distinct representatives, such as $x_1^q$ and $x_1$, induce the same
   367		function. Statements phrased in terms of $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ retain the
   368		representative convention of Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc}.
   369	\end{definition}

   371	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz--Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]\label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   372		\lean{MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.schwartzZippel_totalDegree}
   373		\leanok
   374		% Restatement of lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree under the source's label.
   375		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   376		Let $f, g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials of total degree at
   377		most $d$. Then
   378		\[
   379			\Prb_{\bx \sim \F_q^m}[f(\bx) = g(\bx)] \le \frac{d}{q}\;.
   380		\]
   381	\end{lemma}
   382	\begin{proof}
   383		\leanok
   384		\uses{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}
   385		This is Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}, stated and proved in
   386		Chapter~\ref{chap:preliminaries}; it is restated here under the label used
   387		by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   388	\end{proof}
   389	
   390	\begin{remark}\label{rem:schwartz-zippel-restated}
   391		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel} restates the total-degree bound of
   392		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree} under the label used by
   393		\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}. The individual-degree consequence,
   394		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-individual}, shows that distinct elements of
   395		$\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ agree on at most an $md/q$ fraction of the points of
   396		$\F_q^m$; the analysis of the Pauli basis test uses the bound in this
   397		individual-degree form.
   398	\end{remark}
   399	
   400	The Schwartz--Zippel lemma implies that low-degree polynomials form an
   401	error-correcting code with good distance, the \emph{low-degree code} (a special
   402	case of the generalized Reed--Muller code).
   403	
   404	\begin{definition}[Low-degree encoding]\label{def:low-degree-encoding}
   405		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   406		Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$. For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$
   407		define the $m$-variate multilinear polynomial over $\F_q$
   408		\[
   409			\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)
   410			= \prod_{i : y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i : y_i = 0} (1 - x_i)\;,
   411		\]
   412		identifying $\{0,1\}$ with a subset of $\F_q$. Restricted to the subcube
   413		$\{0,1\}^m$, the polynomial $\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}$ vanishes everywhere except
   414		at $x = y$, where it equals $1$. For $a \in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates
   415		of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ (identifying $\{0,1\}^m$ with
   416		$\{1, \dots, M\}$ by the lexicographic ordering). The \emph{low-degree
   417		encoding of $a$} is the multilinear polynomial $g_a : \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   418		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   419		\begin{equation}\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   420			g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\;.
   421		\end{equation}
   422		For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ one has $g_a(y) = a_y$, and $g_a$ has total
   423		degree at most $m$.
   424	\end{definition}
   425	
   426	\begin{definition}[Indicator vector and linearity of the encoding]\label{def:indicator-vector}
   427		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   428		For $x \in \F_q^m$, the \emph{indicator vector} is
   429		\[
   430			\mathrm{ind}_m(x)
   431			= \bigl(\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\bigr)_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} \in \F_q^M\;.
   432		\]
   433		With this notation the low-degree encoding satisfies, for every
   434		$a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$,
   435		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   436		\begin{equation}\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   437			g_a(x) = a \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(x)\;;
   438		\end{equation}
   439		in particular the map $a \mapsto g_a$ is $\F_q$-linear.
   440	\end{definition}
   441	
   442	Since encodings $g_a$ are multilinear, hence of total degree at most $m$, two
   443	encodings of distinct strings agree on at most an $m/q$ fraction of points of
   444	$\F_q^m$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel}.
   445	
   446	\begin{definition}[Decoding maps]\label{def:decoding-map}
   447		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.decodeAt, MIPStarRE.QPBT.decodeBool, MIPStarRE.QPBT.decodeAt_lowDegreeEnc}
   448		\leanok

   450		For $H \subseteq \F_q$, the \emph{decoding map} $\mathrm{Dec}_H$ takes as
   451		input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and returns the vector
   452		$a \in \F_q^M$ defined by: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, set $a_y = g(y)$ if
   453		$g(y) \in H$, and $a_y = 0$ otherwise. For all $a \in H^M$ one has
   454		$\mathrm{Dec}_H(g_a) = a$. We write $\mathrm{Dec}(\cdot)$ for the boolean
   455		decoding map $\mathrm{Dec}_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.
   456	\end{definition}

    12	\title{The Cross-Basis Phase in the Extracted Pauli Observables}
    13	\author{}
    14	\date{2026-09-03}
    15	
    16	\begin{document}
    17	\maketitle
    18	
    19	\section{At a glance}
    20	
    21	\begin{itemize}
    22	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Low.  The source drops a nontrivial phase when the
    23	  two binary-basis indices are distinct.
    24	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} One exact multiplication calculation for
    25	  generalized Pauli observables; no robustness estimate changes.
    26	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Finite-sum bilinearity and the field
    27	  trace are standard algebra.  The extracted-observable product form and the
    28	  project's phase convention are project-local.
    29	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} The generalized Pauli commutation
    30	  relation and nondegeneracy of the trace pairing.  The local correction is
    31	  tracked in \ghissue{19}.
    32	\end{itemize}
    33	
    34	\section{Key theorem forms}
    35	
    36	Let $e_1,\ldots,e_t$ be the fixed self-dual basis of $\mathbb F_q$ over
    37	$\mathbb F_2$.  With the phase convention of the source, generalized Pauli
    38	observables satisfy
    39	\[
    40	  \tau^X(a)\tau^Z(b)
    41	  =(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}(a\mathbin{\cdot}b)}
    42	   \tau^Z(b)\tau^X(a).
    43	\]
    44	Substituting $a=e_j\widetilde u$ and $b=e_{j'}\widetilde v$ gives the exact
    45	relation
    46	\[
    47	  \widetilde X^j(\widetilde u)\widetilde Z^{j'}(\widetilde v)
    48	  =(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}
    49	      (e_je_{j'}(\widetilde u\mathbin{\cdot}\widetilde v))}
    50	   \widetilde Z^{j'}(\widetilde v)\widetilde X^j(\widetilde u).
    51	\]
    52	This formula applies uniformly, whether or not $j=j'$.
    53	
    54	\section{The false dichotomy in the source}
    55	
    56	Lines~1438--1450 of
    57	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}
    58	identify each extracted observable with a tensor product containing
    59	$\tau^W(e_j\widetilde u)$.  Lines~1451--1456 then claim that the extracted
    60	$X$- and $Z$-observables commute whenever $j\neq j'$
    61	\cite[lines~1438--1456]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  Self-duality gives only
    62	\[
    63	  \operatorname{tr}(e_je_{j'})=0 \qquad (j\neq j').
    64	\]
    65	It does not imply
    66	\[
    67	  \operatorname{tr}(e_je_{j'}s)=0
    68	  \qquad\text{for every }s\in\mathbb F_q.
    69	\]
    70	
    71	Indeed, for distinct $j,j'$, the element $c=e_je_{j'}$ is nonzero.  The trace
    72	pairing is nondegenerate, so there is an $s\in\mathbb F_q$ for which
    73	$\operatorname{tr}(cs)=1$.  Taking vectors whose first coordinates are $1$
    74	and $s$, with all remaining coordinates zero, gives
    75	$\widetilde u\mathbin{\cdot}\widetilde v=s$.  The two extracted observables
    76	then anticommute.  This is a counterexample to the printed cross-basis
    77	commutation assertion.
    78	
    79	When $\widetilde u\mathbin{\cdot}\widetilde v$ lies in the prime field, the
    80	printed distinction is recovered from self-duality.  The chapter quantifies
    81	over arbitrary vectors, however, so that special case does not repair its
    82	statement.
    83	
    84	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
    85	
    86	The discussion following the product-form calculation in
    87	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex}, lines~69--95, records
    88	the full phase and notes that the false dichotomy is not used later in the
    89	extraction argument.  A formal theorem may therefore retain the mathematically
    90	correct uniform phase relation with a \textbf{Local fix} marker.  It must not
    91	assert exact commutation merely from $j\neq j'$.
    92	
    93	This correction changes neither the definition of the extracted observables
    94	nor the source-faithful consistency and extraction conclusions.  It repairs an
    95	auxiliary algebraic assertion that is independent of the robustness estimates.
    96	
    97	\section{Conclusion}
    98	
    99	The source's cross-basis commutation claim is false for general
   100	$\widetilde u$ and $\widetilde v$.  The correct relation retains the phase
   101	$(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}(e_je_{j'}(\widetilde u\cdot\widetilde v))}$.
   102	Because the later argument does not invoke the false dichotomy, this is a
   103	local correction rather than an additional hypothesis on the extraction
   104	theorem.
