    12	\title{The Decoding Identity in the Pauli Extraction Argument}
    13	\author{}
    14	\date{2026-09-03}
    15	
    16	\begin{document}
    17	\maketitle
    18	
    19	\section{At a glance}
    20	
    21	\begin{itemize}
    22	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The source applies a decoder--encoder
    23	  identity to every bounded individual-degree polynomial, although the identity
    24	  is guaranteed for encoded polynomials and can fail outside the encoding image.
    25	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} One restricted algebraic identity and one
    26	  probabilistic estimate showing that the constructed measurement assigns
    27	  little state-dependent mass to outcomes outside the encoding image.
    28	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Evaluation of the multilinear
    29	  interpolant is elementary polynomial algebra.  The non-encoding-mass bound
    30	  uses project-specific consistency estimates and Schwartz--Zippel.
    31	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} Multilinear interpolation on the
    32	  Boolean cube, injectivity of the low-degree encoding, measurement
    33	  consistency, and Schwartz--Zippel.  The correction is tracked in
    34	  \ghissue{19}.
    35	\end{itemize}
    36	
    37	\section{Key theorem forms}
    38	
    39	For a word $h\colon\{0,1\}^m\to\mathbb F_q$, let $g_h$ be its multilinear
    40	extension.  Define the chapter's decoder by
    41	\[
    42	  \operatorname{Dec}(g)(y)=g(y),
    43	  \qquad y\in\{0,1\}^m.
    44	\]
    45	Then
    46	\[
    47	  \operatorname{Dec}(g_h)=h
    48	  \quad\text{and}\quad
    49	  \operatorname{Dec}(g_h)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_m(u)=g_h(u).
    50	\]
    51	More generally, the second identity holds for a polynomial outcome $g$ under
    52	the explicit hypothesis that $g$ belongs to the image of the encoding; no
    53	converse is asserted.
    54	
    55	For an arbitrary bounded individual-degree polynomial $g$, the Boolean values
    56	determine its multilinear interpolant, not necessarily $g$ itself.  The
    57	unrestricted identity
    58	\[
    59	  \operatorname{Dec}(g)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_m(u)=g(u)
    60	\]
    61	is therefore false.
    62	
    63	\section{Counterexample and source comparison}
    64	
    65	The low-degree encoding is defined at lines~873--897 of
    66	\path{references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex}.  The general decoder at
    67	lines~917--924 retains evaluations lying in a chosen subset $H$; the extraction
    68	chapter instead specifies at lines~1419--1420 of
    69	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex} that the
    70	decoder returns all evaluations on the Boolean cube.  This is the specialization
    71	$H=\mathbb F_q$, rather than the Boolean-valued shorthand used earlier
    72	\cite[lines~873--924 and 1419--1420]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
    73	
    74	Take $m=1$, $d\geq2$, and a field of characteristic two with more than two
    75	elements.  For $g(x)=x^2$, the Boolean evaluations are $g(0)=0$ and $g(1)=1$.
    76	Consequently the decoder is the word whose multilinear extension is $x$.
    77	For any $u\notin\{0,1\}$ with $u^2\neq u$,
    78	\[
    79	  \operatorname{Dec}(g)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_1(u)=u
    80	  \neq u^2=g(u).
    81	\]
    82	Thus the equality asserted for every $g$ at lines~1483--1492 of the chapter-14
    83	source mirror is false \cite[lines~1483--1492]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  If degrees at
    84	least $q$ are allowed, equality as a function would not by itself prove encoding
    85	membership either, since $x^q$ and $x$ induce the same function on $\mathbb F_q$.
    86	
    87	\section{Required repair}
    88	
    89	The extraction proof must split the marginal measurement into encoding and
    90	non-encoding outcomes.  On encoding outcomes, the restricted identity above
    91	justifies the substitution.  On the complement, the proof must bound
    92	\[
    93	  \sum_{g\ \mathrm{not\ an\ encoding}}
    94	  \langle\widehat\psi,\widehat S_g^W\widehat\psi\rangle.
    95	\]
    96	The blueprint derives an $O(\delta_S)+md/q$ bound from point consistency and
    97	the combined point measurement.  A non-encoding polynomial differs from every
    98	encoded polynomial, so Schwartz--Zippel bounds the probability that their
    99	evaluations coincide.  This estimate is the open reduction; it must be proved
   100	from the paper hypotheses rather than inserted as an extraction hypothesis.
   101	
   102	The conjugation calculation at lines~1805--1822 does not require the false
   103	unrestricted identity.  Its decoder term cancels against the outcome shift,
   104	and only linearity of $h\mapsto g_h$ and the genuine identity
   105	$\operatorname{Dec}(g_h)=h$ are needed
   106	\cite[lines~1805--1822]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   107	
   108	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
   109	
   110	The decoding-identity remark and the proof of the pulled-apart consistency
   111	lemma in
   112	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex} state the restricted
   113	identity and isolate the non-encoding-mass estimate.  The Lean API should
   114	therefore require encoding membership at every use of the dot-product
   115	evaluation theorem.  No unrestricted theorem, residual assumption, or witness
   116	field is source-faithful.
   117	
   118	\section{Conclusion}
   119	
   120	The decoding identity is false for a general polynomial outcome.  Restricting
   121	it to the encoding image is a necessary local correction.  Recovering the
   122	source's measurement-consistency conclusion then requires the separate
   123	non-encoding-mass estimate, which remains an open proof obligation.

    13	\author{}
    14	\date{2026-09-03}
    15	
    16	\begin{document}
    17	\maketitle
    18	
    19	\section{At a glance}
    20	
    21	\begin{itemize}
    22	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The source quotes a fiberwise consequence
    23	  of a state-dependent quantum linearity theorem, but suppresses two averages
    24	  and a compatibility argument for the auxiliary spaces.
    25	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} One faithful theorem for a single family,
    26	  followed by a finite common-extension construction that makes the auxiliary space
    27	  uniform over the outer parameters.
    28	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Finite direct sums, extensions of
    29	  operators, and squared norms are standard linear algebra.  The imported
    30	  quantum linearity theorem and its state-dependent metric are project-level
    31	  inputs.
    32	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} Theorem~10 of
    33	  \cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}, finite averaging, and extension by the identity
    34	  on orthogonal summands.  This reduction is tracked in
    35	  \ghissue{19}.
    36	\end{itemize}
    37	
    38	\section{Key theorem forms}
    39	
    40	Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let $\rho$ be an arbitrary
    41	density operator on $H$, and let $u\mapsto O^u$ be binary observables on $H$,
    42	indexed by $\mathbb F_2^t$.  The cited theorem assumes the averaged
    43	correlation estimate
    44	\[
    45	  \mathop{\mathbb E}_{u,v}
    46	  \operatorname{Tr}\!\left(O^u O^v O^{u+v}\rho\right) \geq 1-\delta.
    47	\]
    48	It produces an auxiliary space $H'$, a unit vector $\mathrm{anc}\in H'$, and
    49	binary observables $L^u$ on $H\otimes H'$ satisfying, with
    50	$\rho'=\rho\otimes|\mathrm{anc}\rangle\langle\mathrm{anc}|$,
    51	\[
    52	  L^uL^v=L^{u+v}
    53	  \quad\text{for every }u,v.
    54	\]
    55	Moreover,
    56	\[
    57	  \mathop{\mathbb E}_{u}
    58	  \operatorname{Tr}\!\left((L^u-O^u\otimes I_{H'})^\dagger
    59	    (L^u-O^u\otimes I_{H'})\,\rho'\right)\leq\delta.
    60	\]
    61	In particular, $L^0=I$: exact linearity gives $(L^0)^2=L^0$, while an
    62	observable is invertible.
    63	
    64	The chapter needs a parameterized version.  For each pair $(x,z)$ it applies
    65	the theorem to $(r,s)\mapsto O^{x,z,r,s}$.  Since the provider theorem accepts
    66	the actual nonnegative defect on each fiber, no assumption that a fiber defect
    67	is at most one, and no good--bad fiber split, is needed.  One must still
    68	formulate the finite common-extension step that makes the auxiliary space
    69	uniform over $(x,z)$.
    70	
    71	\section{Comparison with the quoted statement}
    72	
    73	Lines~711--725 of
    74	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex} quote the
    75	linearity theorem.  The displayed hypothesis correctly averages over both
    76	group variables.  The displayed conclusion, however, says that the corrected
    77	observable is close for every $u$, whereas Theorem~10 of the cited work gives
    78	closeness only on average over $u$ \cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}.  The quotation
    79	also inserts $\delta\leq1$, which is absent from the provider theorem and would
    80	unnecessarily obstruct applying it with a fiber's actual defect.  The assertion
    81	at the identity follows from exact linearity as above.
    82	
    83	Lines~825--832 construct the family $O^{x,z,r,s}$ and establish approximate
    84	linearity only after averaging over $x,z,r,r',s,s'$.  They then apply the
    85	single-family theorem separately for every $(x,z)$ and state that sufficiently
    86	many zero ancillas avoid a further extension.  The remaining implicit step is
    87	to make the theorem's possibly fiber-dependent auxiliary spaces uniform.
    88	
    89	The finite setting admits a standard repair.  Apply the theorem on each fiber
    90	with its actual defect, choose one finite auxiliary space large enough for all
    91	returned spaces, and embed each returned space so that its unit vector maps to
    92	one fixed vector.  Extend the conjugated observables by the identity on the
    93	orthogonal complement.  The embeddings may depend on the fiber because the
    94	observables do.  Averaging then yields the conclusion used later in the
    95	chapter.  This is an open reduction, not a counterexample to the quoted theorem
    96	or to the source's eventual combined-measurement conclusion.
    97	
    98	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
    99	
   100	The blueprint records the averaged theorem form and the common-ancilla
   101	obligation in
   102	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex}, lines~82--180.  No
   103	source-labelled Lean theorem should assert pointwise closeness or a common
   104	auxiliary space until that finite-family reduction has been proved.
   105	The chapter-16 extraction statements may consume the resulting global-pair
   106	witness once the reduction is discharged; they must not assume a new
   107	fiberwise linearity hypothesis.
   108	
   109	\section{Conclusion}
   110	
   111	The primary discrepancy is a quantifier mismatch in the quotation: the cited
   112	linearity theorem gives average, not pointwise, closeness.  Its use for the
   113	family indexed by $(x,z)$ also requires an explicit finite common-extension
   114	argument.  Both are open formal reductions compatible with the intended
   115	source conclusion.

    38	\section{Key theorem forms}
    39	
    40	Let $H_X$ and $H_Z$ be the positive contractions of the extraction proof, and
    41	let $\vartheta$ be a unit vector such that
    42	\[
    43	  \langle\vartheta,H_W\vartheta\rangle\geq1-\delta/2
    44	  \qquad (W\in\{X,Z\}).
    45	\]
    46	Since $(I-H_W)^2\geq0$,
    47	\[
    48	  H_W^2\geq2H_W-I,
    49	  \qquad
    50	  \langle\vartheta,H_W^2\vartheta\rangle\geq1-\delta.
    51	\]
    52	Also $\lVert(I-H_W)\vartheta\rVert^2\leq\delta$, whence
    53	\[
    54	  \lVert H_X\vartheta-H_Z\vartheta\rVert^2\leq4\delta.
    55	\]
    56	Together with $H_XH_Z$ equal to the EPR projection, these estimates give the
    57	required overlap bound, with constants absorbed into the stated
    58	$O(\sqrt\delta)$ error.
    59	
    60	For the final transfer, let $\phi\colon\mathcal H\to\mathcal K$ be an isometry
    61	and set $Q=\phi\phi^\dagger$.  If $N_h$ is the unitary-conjugated extension of
    62	a measurement operator $M_h$, then the exact identity is
    63	\[
    64	  \phi M_h\phi^\dagger=N_hQ=QN_h,
    65	\]
    66	not merely $N_h$.  Thus comparison of $N_h$ with an ideal projector must be
    67	combined with control of $(I-Q)\Delta$ on the ideal comparison state
    68	$\Delta$.

    70	\section{Numerical defects in the source proof}
    71	
    72	Lines~1715--1742 of
    73	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}
    74	construct $H_X,H_Z$ and identify $H_XH_Z$ with the EPR projection.  The norm
    75	estimate at lines~1743--1750 gives
    76	$\lVert(I-H_W)\vartheta\rVert\leq\sqrt\delta$.  At lines~1753--1757 the
    77	source substitutes $\delta$ inside the reverse triangle inequality
    78	\cite[lines~1715--1783]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  That replacement is not valid for
    79	small $\delta$.  The desired lower bound on
    80	$\langle H_W^2\rangle$ follows directly from $H_W^2\geq2H_W-I$, as above.
    81	
    82	The triangle inequality yields
    83	\[
    84	  \lVert H_X\vartheta-H_Z\vartheta\rVert\leq2\sqrt\delta,
    85	\]
    86	so its square is at most $4\delta$.  Line~1761 instead bounds that square by
    87	$2\sqrt\delta$ without a stated restriction.  This inequality follows when
    88	$\delta\leq1/4$; for larger error the theorem is made trivial by enlarging the
    89	universal constant.  The same small-error split ensures that the projected
    90	vector defined at lines~1769--1773 is nonzero before it is normalized.  These
    91	are local numerical repairs and do not weaken the extraction conclusion.
    92	
    93	\section{The range-projection obligation}
    94	
    95	Lines~1827--1858 prove state-dependent closeness for the concrete operators
    96	obtained by conjugating the original measurement with the swap unitaries.
    97	Lines~1864--1875 then define isometries by adjoining EPR pairs and applying
    98	those unitaries, and immediately state the corresponding closeness for
    99	$\phi M_h\phi^\dagger$.  The omitted range projection makes this implication
   100	non-definitional \cite[lines~1827--1875]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   101	
   102	Let $\Psi$ be the original state and suppose $\phi\Psi$ is close to the ideal
   103	state $\Delta$.  Since $Q\phi\Psi=\phi\Psi$ and $Q$ is a contraction, the
   104	triangle inequality bounds $(I-Q)\Delta$ by the state-extraction error.  Using
   105	$\phi M_h\phi^\dagger=N_hQ$, split
   106	\[
   107	  (N_hQ-T_h)\Delta
   108	  =(N_h-T_h)\Delta-N_h(I-Q)\Delta,
   109	\]
   110	where $T_h$ is the ideal Pauli projector.  Summing squared norms over $h$
   111	uses projectivity and orthogonality to keep the second term under control.
   112	The same argument is required for each player and each Pauli basis.
   113	
   114	This transfer is an open proof obligation for the next extraction stage.  It
   115	must be a theorem derived from the concrete swap unitaries, transformed-state
   116	estimate, and operator comparisons.  It must not be stored as a bridge field,
   117	residual assumption, or hypothesis of the source-labelled soundness theorem.

   119	\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
   120	
   121	The proof of the extraction lemma in
   122	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex}, lines~267--274, uses the
   123	correct positive-contraction estimate and explicit small-error convention.
   124	Lines~299--330 isolate the range projection and give the transfer strategy.
   125	The chapter therefore preserves the source's state and observable conclusions
   126	while exposing the missing argument.  Stage~4.2 should provide only the
   127	concrete extraction data and comparison theorems; the range-projection lemma
   128	belongs to Stage~4.3.
   129	
   130	\section{Conclusion}
   131	
   132	The printed triangle calculation has repairable numerical errors, and the
   133	last passage from unitaries to isometries omits a genuine range-projection
   134	argument.  Neither defect is a counterexample to Pauli soundness.  The former
   135	is corrected by positive-contraction inequalities and a small-error split;
   136	the latter remains a named downstream proof obligation whose hypotheses are
   137	already supplied by the extraction lemma.

    98	\begin{theorem}[Quantum linearity test~\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}]
    99		\label{thm:linearity}
   100		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.IsBinaryObservable, MIPStarRE.QPBT.stateDepDistSq}

   103		\uses{def:povm-conventions}
   104		Let $t$ be a positive integer and $\delta \ge 0$. Let $\rho$ be a
   105		density operator on a Hilbert space $\hilb$ and let
   106		$\{\mathcal{O}^u\}$ be a set of binary observables indexed by
   107		$u \in \F_2^t$ acting on $\hilb$, such that on average over $u, u'$
   108		chosen uniformly at random from $\F_2^t$,
   109		\[
   110			\E_{u,u'} \Tr\big(\mathcal{O}^u \, \mathcal{O}^{u'} \,
   111			\mathcal{O}^{u+u'} \, \rho\big) \ge 1 - \delta\,.
   112		\]
   113		Then there exist a Hilbert space $\hilb'$, a pure state
   114		$\ket{\mathrm{anc}} \in \hilb'$, and binary observables
   115		$\{\mathcal{L}^u\}$ indexed by $u \in \F_2^t$ acting on
   116		$\hilb \ot \hilb'$ such that, writing
   117		$\rho' = \rho \ot \ket{\mathrm{anc}}\bra{\mathrm{anc}}$, the exact
   118		linearity
   119		\[
   120			\mathcal{L}^u \, \mathcal{L}^{u'} = \mathcal{L}^{u+u'}
   121		\]
   122		holds for all $u, u' \in \F_2^t$, and
   123		\[
   124			\E_{u} \, d_{\rho'}\big(\mathcal{L}^u,\ \mathcal{O}^u \ot
   125			\Id_{\hilb'}\big)^2 \le \delta\,,
   126		\]
   127		where the expectation is over $u$ chosen uniformly at random from
   128		$\F_2^t$ and
   129		$d_{\sigma}(S,T)
   130		= \big(\Tr\big((S-T)^\dagger (S-T)\, \sigma\big)\big)^{1/2}$
   131		denotes the state-dependent distance with respect to a density
   132		operator $\sigma$.
   133	\end{theorem}

+\documentclass[11pt]{article}
+
+\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb}
+\usepackage{xurl}
+\usepackage[hidelinks]{hyperref}
+\setlength{\emergencystretch}{2em}
+
+\input{command}
+\renewcommand{\ghissue}[1]{%
+  \href{https://github.com/Dengnifer/MIPStarRE-A/issues/#1}{GitHub issue \##1}}
+
+\title{The Cross-Basis Phase in the Extracted Pauli Observables}
+\author{}
+\date{2026-09-03}
+
+\begin{document}
+\maketitle
+
+\section{At a glance}
+
+\begin{itemize}
+  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Low.  The source drops a nontrivial phase when the
+  two binary-basis indices are distinct.
+  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} One exact multiplication calculation for
+  generalized Pauli observables; no robustness estimate changes.
+  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Finite-sum bilinearity and the field
+  trace are standard algebra.  The extracted-observable product form and the
+  project's phase convention are project-local.
+  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} The generalized Pauli commutation
+  relation and nondegeneracy of the trace pairing.  The local correction is
+  tracked in \ghissue{19}.
+\end{itemize}
+
+\section{Key theorem forms}
+
+Let $e_1,\ldots,e_t$ be the fixed self-dual basis of $\mathbb F_q$ over
+$\mathbb F_2$.  With the phase convention of the source, generalized Pauli
+observables satisfy
+\[
+  \tau^X(a)\tau^Z(b)
+  =(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}(a\mathbin{\cdot}b)}
+   \tau^Z(b)\tau^X(a).
+\]
+Substituting $a=e_j\widetilde u$ and $b=e_{j'}\widetilde v$ gives the exact
+relation
+\[
+  \widetilde X^j(\widetilde u)\widetilde Z^{j'}(\widetilde v)
+  =(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}
+      (e_je_{j'}(\widetilde u\mathbin{\cdot}\widetilde v))}
+   \widetilde Z^{j'}(\widetilde v)\widetilde X^j(\widetilde u).
+\]
+This formula applies uniformly, whether or not $j=j'$.
+
+\section{The false dichotomy in the source}
+
+Lines~1438--1450 of
+\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}
+identify each extracted observable with a tensor product containing
+$\tau^W(e_j\widetilde u)$.  Lines~1451--1456 then claim that the extracted
+$X$- and $Z$-observables commute whenever $j\neq j'$
+\cite[lines~1438--1456]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  Self-duality gives only
+\[
+  \operatorname{tr}(e_je_{j'})=0 \qquad (j\neq j').
+\]
+It does not imply
+\[
+  \operatorname{tr}(e_je_{j'}s)=0
+  \qquad\text{for every }s\in\mathbb F_q.
+\]
+
+Indeed, for distinct $j,j'$, the element $c=e_je_{j'}$ is nonzero.  The trace
+pairing is nondegenerate, so there is an $s\in\mathbb F_q$ for which
+$\operatorname{tr}(cs)=1$.  Taking vectors whose first coordinates are $1$
+and $s$, with all remaining coordinates zero, gives
+$\widetilde u\mathbin{\cdot}\widetilde v=s$.  The two extracted observables
+then anticommute.  This is a counterexample to the printed cross-basis
+commutation assertion.
+
+When $\widetilde u\mathbin{\cdot}\widetilde v$ lies in the prime field, the
+printed distinction is recovered from self-duality.  The chapter quantifies
+over arbitrary vectors, however, so that special case does not repair its
+statement.
+
+\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
+
+The discussion following the product-form calculation in
+\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex}, lines~69--95, records
+the full phase and notes that the false dichotomy is not used later in the
+extraction argument.  A formal theorem may therefore retain the mathematically
+correct uniform phase relation with a \textbf{Local fix} marker.  It must not
+assert exact commutation merely from $j\neq j'$.
+
+This correction changes neither the definition of the extracted observables
+nor the source-faithful consistency and extraction conclusions.  It repairs an
+auxiliary algebraic assertion that is independent of the robustness estimates.
+
+\section{Conclusion}
+
+The source's cross-basis commutation claim is false for general
+$\widetilde u$ and $\widetilde v$.  The correct relation retains the phase
+$(-1)^{\operatorname{tr}(e_je_{j'}(\widetilde u\cdot\widetilde v))}$.
+Because the later argument does not invoke the false dichotomy, this is a
+local correction rather than an additional hypothesis on the extraction
+theorem.
+
+\bibliographystyle{alpha}
+\bibliography{references}
+
+\end{document}

+\documentclass[11pt]{article}
+
+\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb}
+\usepackage{xurl}
+\usepackage[hidelinks]{hyperref}
+\setlength{\emergencystretch}{2em}
+
+\input{command}
+\renewcommand{\ghissue}[1]{%
+  \href{https://github.com/Dengnifer/MIPStarRE-A/issues/#1}{GitHub issue \##1}}
+
+\title{The Decoding Identity in the Pauli Extraction Argument}
+\author{}
+\date{2026-09-03}
+
+\begin{document}
+\maketitle
+
+\section{At a glance}
+
+\begin{itemize}
+  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The source applies a decoder--encoder
+  identity to every bounded individual-degree polynomial, although the identity
+  is guaranteed for encoded polynomials and can fail outside the encoding image.
+  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} One restricted algebraic identity and one
+  probabilistic estimate showing that the constructed measurement assigns
+  little state-dependent mass to outcomes outside the encoding image.
+  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Evaluation of the multilinear
+  interpolant is elementary polynomial algebra.  The non-encoding-mass bound
+  uses project-specific consistency estimates and Schwartz--Zippel.
+  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} Multilinear interpolation on the
+  Boolean cube, injectivity of the low-degree encoding, measurement
+  consistency, and Schwartz--Zippel.  The correction is tracked in
+  \ghissue{19}.
+\end{itemize}
+
+\section{Key theorem forms}
+
+For a word $h\colon\{0,1\}^m\to\mathbb F_q$, let $g_h$ be its multilinear
+extension.  Define the chapter's decoder by
+\[
+  \operatorname{Dec}(g)(y)=g(y),
+  \qquad y\in\{0,1\}^m.
+\]
+Then
+\[
+  \operatorname{Dec}(g_h)=h
+  \quad\text{and}\quad
+  \operatorname{Dec}(g_h)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_m(u)=g_h(u).
+\]
+More generally, the second identity holds for a polynomial outcome $g$ under
+the explicit hypothesis that $g$ belongs to the image of the encoding; no
+converse is asserted.
+
+For an arbitrary bounded individual-degree polynomial $g$, the Boolean values
+determine its multilinear interpolant, not necessarily $g$ itself.  The
+unrestricted identity
+\[
+  \operatorname{Dec}(g)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_m(u)=g(u)
+\]
+is therefore false.
+
+\section{Counterexample and source comparison}
+
+The low-degree encoding is defined at lines~873--897 of
+\path{references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex}.  The general decoder at
+lines~917--924 retains evaluations lying in a chosen subset $H$; the extraction
+chapter instead specifies at lines~1419--1420 of
+\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex} that the
+decoder returns all evaluations on the Boolean cube.  This is the specialization
+$H=\mathbb F_q$, rather than the Boolean-valued shorthand used earlier
+\cite[lines~873--924 and 1419--1420]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
+
+Take $m=1$, $d\geq2$, and a field of characteristic two with more than two
+elements.  For $g(x)=x^2$, the Boolean evaluations are $g(0)=0$ and $g(1)=1$.
+Consequently the decoder is the word whose multilinear extension is $x$.
+For any $u\notin\{0,1\}$ with $u^2\neq u$,
+\[
+  \operatorname{Dec}(g)\mathbin{\cdot}\operatorname{ind}_1(u)=u
+  \neq u^2=g(u).
+\]
+Thus the equality asserted for every $g$ at lines~1483--1492 of the chapter-14
+source mirror is false \cite[lines~1483--1492]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  If degrees at
+least $q$ are allowed, equality as a function would not by itself prove encoding
+membership either, since $x^q$ and $x$ induce the same function on $\mathbb F_q$.
+
+\section{Required repair}
+
+The extraction proof must split the marginal measurement into encoding and
+non-encoding outcomes.  On encoding outcomes, the restricted identity above
+justifies the substitution.  On the complement, the proof must bound
+\[
+  \sum_{g\ \mathrm{not\ an\ encoding}}
+  \langle\widehat\psi,\widehat S_g^W\widehat\psi\rangle.
+\]
+The blueprint derives an $O(\delta_S)+md/q$ bound from point consistency and
+the combined point measurement.  A non-encoding polynomial differs from every
+encoded polynomial, so Schwartz--Zippel bounds the probability that their
+evaluations coincide.  This estimate is the open reduction; it must be proved
+from the paper hypotheses rather than inserted as an extraction hypothesis.
+
+The conjugation calculation at lines~1805--1822 does not require the false
+unrestricted identity.  Its decoder term cancels against the outcome shift,
+and only linearity of $h\mapsto g_h$ and the genuine identity
+$\operatorname{Dec}(g_h)=h$ are needed
+\cite[lines~1805--1822]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
+
+\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
+
+The decoding-identity remark and the proof of the pulled-apart consistency
+lemma in
+\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex} state the restricted
+identity and isolate the non-encoding-mass estimate.  The Lean API should
+therefore require encoding membership at every use of the dot-product
+evaluation theorem.  No unrestricted theorem, residual assumption, or witness
+field is source-faithful.
+
+\section{Conclusion}
+
+The decoding identity is false for a general polynomial outcome.  Restricting

+\documentclass[11pt]{article}
+
+\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb}
+\usepackage{xurl}

+\setlength{\emergencystretch}{2em}

+
+\title{Triangle Estimates and Isometry Transfer in Pauli Extraction}
+\author{}
+\date{2026-09-03}
+
+\begin{document}
+\maketitle
+
+\section{At a glance}
+
+\begin{itemize}
+  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The extraction proof contains two
+  incorrect numerical steps and later suppresses the range projection when
+  passing from unitary conjugation to isometry conjugation.
+  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} A corrected positive-contraction estimate,
+  a small-error case split for normalization, and one range-projection transfer
+  lemma for a projective measurement family.
+  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Positivity, contraction inequalities,
+  isometry range projections, and norm estimates belong to finite-dimensional
+  Hilbert-space algebra.  The state-dependent family distance and register
+  placements are project-local.
+  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} The inequality
+  $H^2\geq2H-I$ for a positive contraction, the triangle inequality, and
+  $Q=\phi\phi^\dagger$ for an isometry.  The repair is tracked in
+  \ghissue{19}.
+\end{itemize}
+
+\section{Key theorem forms}
+
+Let $H_X$ and $H_Z$ be the positive contractions of the extraction proof, and
+let $\vartheta$ be a unit vector such that
+\[
+  \langle\vartheta,H_W\vartheta\rangle\geq1-\delta/2
+  \qquad (W\in\{X,Z\}).
+\]
+Since $(I-H_W)^2\geq0$,
+\[
+  H_W^2\geq2H_W-I,
+  \qquad
+  \langle\vartheta,H_W^2\vartheta\rangle\geq1-\delta.
+\]
+Also $\lVert(I-H_W)\vartheta\rVert^2\leq\delta$, whence
+\[
+  \lVert H_X\vartheta-H_Z\vartheta\rVert^2\leq4\delta.
+\]
+Together with $H_XH_Z$ equal to the EPR projection, these estimates give the
+required overlap bound, with constants absorbed into the stated
+$O(\sqrt\delta)$ error.
+
+For the final transfer, let $\phi\colon\mathcal H\to\mathcal K$ be an isometry
+and set $Q=\phi\phi^\dagger$.  If $N_h$ is the unitary-conjugated extension of
+a measurement operator $M_h$, then the exact identity is
+\[
+  \phi M_h\phi^\dagger=N_hQ=QN_h,
+\]
+not merely $N_h$.  Thus comparison of $N_h$ with an ideal projector must be
+combined with control of $(I-Q)\Delta$ on the ideal comparison state
+$\Delta$.
+
+\section{Numerical defects in the source proof}
+
+Lines~1715--1742 of
+\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}
+construct $H_X,H_Z$ and identify $H_XH_Z$ with the EPR projection.  The norm
+estimate at lines~1743--1750 gives
+$\lVert(I-H_W)\vartheta\rVert\leq\sqrt\delta$.  At lines~1753--1757 the
+source substitutes $\delta$ inside the reverse triangle inequality
+\cite[lines~1715--1783]{Ji2020MIPStar}.  That replacement is not valid for
+small $\delta$.  The desired lower bound on
+$\langle H_W^2\rangle$ follows directly from $H_W^2\geq2H_W-I$, as above.
+
+The triangle inequality yields
+\[
+  \lVert H_X\vartheta-H_Z\vartheta\rVert\leq2\sqrt\delta,
+\]
+so its square is at most $4\delta$.  Line~1761 instead bounds that square by
+$2\sqrt\delta$ without a stated restriction.  This inequality follows when
+$\delta\leq1/4$; for larger error the theorem is made trivial by enlarging the
+universal constant.  The same small-error split ensures that the projected
+vector defined at lines~1769--1773 is nonzero before it is normalized.  These
+are local numerical repairs and do not weaken the extraction conclusion.
+
+\section{The range-projection obligation}
+
+Lines~1827--1858 prove state-dependent closeness for the concrete operators
+obtained by conjugating the original measurement with the swap unitaries.
+Lines~1864--1875 then define isometries by adjoining EPR pairs and applying
+those unitaries, and immediately state the corresponding closeness for
+$\phi M_h\phi^\dagger$.  The omitted range projection makes this implication
+non-definitional \cite[lines~1827--1875]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
+
+Let $\Psi$ be the original state and suppose $\phi\Psi$ is close to the ideal
+state $\Delta$.  Since $Q\phi\Psi=\phi\Psi$ and $Q$ is a contraction, the
+triangle inequality bounds $(I-Q)\Delta$ by the state-extraction error.  Using
+$\phi M_h\phi^\dagger=N_hQ$, split
+\[
+  (N_hQ-T_h)\Delta
+  =(N_h-T_h)\Delta-N_h(I-Q)\Delta,
+\]
+where $T_h$ is the ideal Pauli projector.  Summing squared norms over $h$
+uses projectivity and orthogonality to keep the second term under control.
+The same argument is required for each player and each Pauli basis.
+
+This transfer is an open proof obligation for the next extraction stage.  It
+must be a theorem derived from the concrete swap unitaries, transformed-state
+estimate, and operator comparisons.  It must not be stored as a bridge field,
+residual assumption, or hypothesis of the source-labelled soundness theorem.
+
+\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
+
+The proof of the extraction lemma in
+\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex}, lines~267--274, uses the
+correct positive-contraction estimate and explicit small-error convention.
+Lines~299--330 isolate the range projection and give the transfer strategy.
+The chapter therefore preserves the source's state and observable conclusions
+while exposing the missing argument.  Stage~4.2 should provide only the
+concrete extraction data and comparison theorems; the range-projection lemma
+belongs to Stage~4.3.
+
+\section{Conclusion}
+
+The printed triangle calculation has repairable numerical errors, and the
+last passage from unitaries to isometries omits a genuine range-projection
+argument.  Neither defect is a counterexample to Pauli soundness.  The former
+is corrected by positive-contraction inequalities and a small-error split;
+the latter remains a named downstream proof obligation whose hypotheses are
+already supplied by the extraction lemma.
+
+\bibliographystyle{alpha}
+\bibliography{references}
+
+\end{document}

+\documentclass[11pt]{article}
+
+\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb}
+\usepackage{xurl}
+\usepackage[hidelinks]{hyperref}
+\setlength{\emergencystretch}{2em}

+\title{The Quoted Quantum Linearity Theorem in the Pauli Basis Analysis}
+\author{}
+\date{2026-09-03}
+
+\begin{document}
+\maketitle
+
+\section{At a glance}
+
+\begin{itemize}
+  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The source quotes a fiberwise consequence
+  of a state-dependent quantum linearity theorem, but suppresses two averages
+  and a compatibility argument for the auxiliary spaces.
+  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} One faithful theorem for a single family,
+  followed by a finite common-extension construction that makes the auxiliary space
+  uniform over the outer parameters.
+  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Finite direct sums, extensions of
+  operators, and squared norms are standard linear algebra.  The imported
+  quantum linearity theorem and its state-dependent metric are project-level
+  inputs.
+  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} Theorem~10 of
+  \cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}, finite averaging, and extension by the identity
+  on orthogonal summands.  This reduction is tracked in
+  \ghissue{19}.
+\end{itemize}
+
+\section{Key theorem forms}
+
+Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, let $\rho$ be an arbitrary
+density operator on $H$, and let $u\mapsto O^u$ be binary observables on $H$,
+indexed by $\mathbb F_2^t$.  The cited theorem assumes the averaged
+correlation estimate
+\[
+  \mathop{\mathbb E}_{u,v}
+  \operatorname{Tr}\!\left(O^u O^v O^{u+v}\rho\right) \geq 1-\delta.
+\]
+It produces an auxiliary space $H'$, a unit vector $\mathrm{anc}\in H'$, and
+binary observables $L^u$ on $H\otimes H'$ satisfying, with
+$\rho'=\rho\otimes|\mathrm{anc}\rangle\langle\mathrm{anc}|$,
+\[
+  L^uL^v=L^{u+v}
+  \quad\text{for every }u,v.
+\]
+Moreover,
+\[
+  \mathop{\mathbb E}_{u}
+  \operatorname{Tr}\!\left((L^u-O^u\otimes I_{H'})^\dagger
+    (L^u-O^u\otimes I_{H'})\,\rho'\right)\leq\delta.
+\]
+In particular, $L^0=I$: exact linearity gives $(L^0)^2=L^0$, while an
+observable is invertible.
+
+The chapter needs a parameterized version.  For each pair $(x,z)$ it applies
+the theorem to $(r,s)\mapsto O^{x,z,r,s}$.  Since the provider theorem accepts
+the actual nonnegative defect on each fiber, no assumption that a fiber defect
+is at most one, and no good--bad fiber split, is needed.  One must still
+formulate the finite common-extension step that makes the auxiliary space
+uniform over $(x,z)$.
+
+\section{Comparison with the quoted statement}
+
+Lines~711--725 of
+\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex} quote the
+linearity theorem.  The displayed hypothesis correctly averages over both
+group variables.  The displayed conclusion, however, says that the corrected
+observable is close for every $u$, whereas Theorem~10 of the cited work gives
+closeness only on average over $u$ \cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}.  The quotation
+also inserts $\delta\leq1$, which is absent from the provider theorem and would
+unnecessarily obstruct applying it with a fiber's actual defect.  The assertion
+at the identity follows from exact linearity as above.
+
+Lines~825--832 construct the family $O^{x,z,r,s}$ and establish approximate
+linearity only after averaging over $x,z,r,r',s,s'$.  They then apply the
+single-family theorem separately for every $(x,z)$ and state that sufficiently
+many zero ancillas avoid a further extension.  The remaining implicit step is
+to make the theorem's possibly fiber-dependent auxiliary spaces uniform.
+
+The finite setting admits a standard repair.  Apply the theorem on each fiber
+with its actual defect, choose one finite auxiliary space large enough for all
+returned spaces, and embed each returned space so that its unit vector maps to
+one fixed vector.  Extend the conjugated observables by the identity on the
+orthogonal complement.  The embeddings may depend on the fiber because the
+observables do.  Averaging then yields the conclusion used later in the
+chapter.  This is an open reduction, not a counterexample to the quoted theorem
+or to the source's eventual combined-measurement conclusion.
+
+\section{Blueprint and formalization status}
+
+The blueprint records the averaged theorem form and the common-ancilla
+obligation in
+\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch15_qpbt_combining.tex}, lines~82--180.  No
+source-labelled Lean theorem should assert pointwise closeness or a common
+auxiliary space until that finite-family reduction has been proved.
+The chapter-16 extraction statements may consume the resulting global-pair
+witness once the reduction is discharged; they must not assume a new
+fiberwise linearity hypothesis.
+
+\section{Conclusion}
+
+The primary discrepancy is a quantifier mismatch in the quotation: the cited
+linearity theorem gives average, not pointwise, closeness.  Its use for the
+family indexed by $(x,z)$ also requires an explicit finite common-extension
+argument.  Both are open formal reductions compatible with the intended
+source conclusion.
+
+\bibliographystyle{alpha}
+\bibliography{references}
+
+\end{document}

## Code review

F1: `decodeOn_univ` is a public data-valued abbreviation, so the repository’s lower-camel-case rule applies. Rename it to `decodeOnUniv` and update `decodeFq`.

- `IsEncoding`, `decodeFq_dotProduct_indicatorVec`, and `nonencodingMarginalMass_le`
- `ExtractionWitness` and `exists_extractionWitness`
- `exists_exactly_linear_observables`

The notes should also explain the apparent tracking split between issue #19 and the Lean docstrings’ issue #47.

F3: The cross-basis note cites blueprint lines 69–95, but the corrected phase is at lines 101–105 and the non-use statement at lines 112–116. The linearity note says lines 82–180 include the common-ancilla obligation, but that obligation is at lines 186–191. These source locators must be refreshed.

The substantive mathematics otherwise checks out. The extraction declarations match the QPBT source’s assumptions and conclusions, with `0 ≤ epsilon ≤ 1` and `0 ≤ deltaG` serving as legitimate error-domain conditions. `ExtractionWitness` packages source conclusions rather than adding a proof-debt input. The explicit `deltaConstructPaulis` and `deltaExtract` scales faithfully expose terms that the paper absorbs into universal constants.

The restricted decoder identity correctly avoids the paper’s false unrestricted interpolation step, and the cross-basis theorem retains the necessary trace phase. The linearity note’s description of the provider theorem is also accurate: Theorem 10 gives exact linearity for all pairs but closeness only on average, without a `δ ≤ 1` premise ([arXiv:1610.03574](https://arxiv.org/html/1610.03574)).

All 26 newly added `sorry` sites are clearly identified as issue #47 proof obligations; no unmarked proof hole or bypass was introduced. Prior findings concerning unitarity fields, projector/completeness declarations, and the helper’s blueprint readiness are resolved. Exact-head local CI is reported green, and `git diff --check` is clean.

## Prose review

The principal equivalence failure is F1. The blueprint fixes one \(C\) in
\(\delta_P=C(\delta_G+\sqrt\epsilon+md/q)\) for all subsequent conclusions. In contrast, `Consistency.lean:49`, `:81`, `:133`, `:159`, `:186`, and `:213` each begin with an independent `∃ C`. These signatures do not formalize the common quantifier. A combined theorem must bind \(C\) before the conjunction of conclusions, or the blueprint must explicitly use distinct constants.

F2 affects every newly linked declaration containing the basis index: `Observables.lean:118`, `:134`, `:154`, `:168`, `:184`, and `:244`, together with `Consistency.lean:218`. For F3, `nonencodingMarginalMass_le` already gives the settled statement at `Consistency.lean:132`. Its unfinished proof does not make the blueprint entry itself unready. Retain the standalone `\lean{...}` without `\leanok`, remove `\notready`, and add the dependencies through `\uses`.

For F5, blueprint lines 15–18 and 28 state precisely the content of `decodeFq_add`, `decodeFq_smul`, `decodeFq_lowDegreeEncoding`, and `decodeFq_dotProduct_indicatorVec` at `Decoding.lean:112`, `:123`, `:136`, and `:151`. These require subordinate traceability entries without `\leanok`; they should not be folded into an existing source-labelled completed block.

For F6, the declarations for the missing properties now exist, but the blueprint still classifies the assertions incorrectly. Projectivity at lines 46, 59, and 72 is theorem content, represented by `marginalPoly_isProjective`, `tauDotProj_isProj`/`sum_tauDotProj_eq_one`, and `tildeM_isProj`/`sum_tildeM_eq_one`. Split those facts from their definition entries.

For F7–F10, use direct mathematical descriptions. For example, replace F7 with “The multilinear encoding as a bounded polynomial representative”; describe F8 as register reassociation, tensor placement, or conjugation; replace F9 by “full-field specialization on polynomial representatives”; and call \(\delta_G\) simply “the global polynomial-pair witness error.” The same “raw” wording also occurs at blueprint lines 15 and 121 and `Defs.lean:239`.

The earlier omission of the two unitarity equations is resolved at `Unitary.lean:45–49`. Counts: 2 equivalence mismatches, 4 status or entry-structure issues, and 4 prose issues.

+# Consistency of the pulled-apart Pauli measurements
+
+This module records the two estimates by which the polynomial marginals absorb
+the expanded point measurements, with both heterogeneous player placements
+written explicitly. It also states the consistency of the pulled-apart
+measurements with the original point measurements and the self-consistency of
+the corresponding observables.
+
+## References
+
+The marginal estimates formalize `lem:qld-constructing-the-paulis-helper` in
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:176-203`, from
+`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1609-1664`.
+The remaining declarations formalize `lem:qld-construct-the-paulis` in
+blueprint lines 105-168, from paper lines 1458-1608.
+-/

+/-! ## Absorption of expanded point measurements -/
+
+/-- The polynomial marginal and the opposite player's expanded point
+measurement resolve the identity on average. The two conjuncts are the
+`AA'`--`BA''` and `BB'`--`AB''` instances of the source's symmetric-equivalents
+clause.
+
+This is Equation `eq:qld-sg-cons` of
+`lem:qld-constructing-the-paulis-helper`, blueprint
+`ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:176-186`, paper
+`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1609-1635`.
+
+**Proof obligation:** issue #19 tracks the agreement calculation converting
+`GlobalPairWitness.point_consistent_alice` and its Bob-side counterpart into
+these two identity estimates. -/
+theorem sum_marginalPoly_pointMeas_approx_id {P : AdmissibleParams}
+    {ε δS : ℝ} {S : ProjectiveSetting P ε} (w : GlobalPairWitness S δS)
+    (W : PauliKind) :
+    opDistSq (uniformDistribution (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P))
+      (fun u => ∑ g : Poly P,
+        S.place .AA' ((w.marginalPoly .alice W).effect g) *
+          S.place .BA''
+            ((S.pointMeasExp .bob W u).effect (MvPolynomial.eval u g.1)))
+      (fun _ => 1) S.psiHat ≤ δS ∧
+    opDistSq (uniformDistribution (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P))
+      (fun u => ∑ g : Poly P,
+        S.place .BB' ((w.marginalPoly .bob W).effect g) *
+          S.place .AB''
+            ((S.pointMeasExp .alice W u).effect (MvPolynomial.eval u g.1)))
+      (fun _ => 1) S.psiHat ≤ δS := by

+/-! ## Consistency of the pulled-apart measurements -/
+
+/-- Alice's original point measurement is consistent with Bob's pulled-apart
+measurement on average over uniformly random points. This is the first display
+of Item 1 in `lem:qld-construct-the-paulis`, blueprint
+`ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:105-122`, paper
+`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1463-1492`.

+theorem tildeM_consistent_pointMeas {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε δS : ℝ}
+    {S : ProjectiveSetting P ε} (w : GlobalPairWitness S δS)
+    (W : PauliKind) :
+    consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P))
+      (fun u a => S.placePlayer .alice ((S.pointMeas .alice W u).effect a))
+      (fun u a => S.placeSide .bob
+        (tildeM w .bob W (indicatorVec u) a))
+      S.psiHat ≤ δS := by
+  sorry

+/-- Alice's pulled-apart measurement is consistent with Bob's original point
+measurement on average over uniformly random points. This is the
+register-interchanged display of Item 1 in `lem:qld-construct-the-paulis`,
+blueprint `ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:105-122`, paper
+`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1463-1492`.
+
+**Proof obligation:** issue #19 tracks the player-interchanged

+    {S : ProjectiveSetting P ε} (w : GlobalPairWitness S δS)
+    (W : PauliKind) :
+    consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P))
+      (fun u a => S.placeSide .alice
+        (tildeM w .alice W (indicatorVec u) a))
+      (fun u a => S.placePlayer .bob ((S.pointMeas .bob W u).effect a))
+      S.psiHat ≤ δS := by
+  sorry
+
+/-- The pulled-apart observables on Alice's and Bob's extraction blocks are
+self-consistent on average over the uniformly random Pauli register. This is
+Item 2 of `lem:qld-construct-the-paulis`, blueprint
+`ch16_qpbt_extraction.tex:123-167`, paper
+`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1476-1605`.
+
+**Proof obligation:** issue #19 tracks the pulling-consistency calculation and
+the final trace postprocessing from measurements to observables. -/
+theorem tildeObs_selfConsistent {P : AdmissibleParams} {ε δS : ℝ}
+    {S : ProjectiveSetting P ε} (w : GlobalPairWitness S δS)
+    (W : PauliKind) (j : Fin P.model.basisDim) :

+      (fun u => S.placeSide .alice (tildeObs w .alice W u j))
+      (fun u => S.placeSide .bob (tildeObs w .bob W u j))
+      S.psiHat ≤ δS := by
+  sorry
+
+end

   228	Displayed equations should be used with restraint.  They are appropriate for the
   229	source estimate being checked, the cited estimate in the form actually used, and
   230	the calculation where a term or hypothesis appears or disappears.  When a
   231	displayed equation is identified by a source label, the label should appear on
   232	the right of the display, while the surrounding prose refers to the mathematical
   233	assertion itself.  The standard \texttt{amsmath} command \verb|\tag| is the
   234	right mechanism for this; a separate local convention should be introduced only
   235	if the standard mechanism is genuinely insufficient.  For a multi-line aligned
   236	display, tag the individual lines that carry the source information rather than
   237	forcing a long combined label below the equations.  Short
   238	scalar definitions and elementary inequalities should remain inline when the
   239	sentence reads better that way.  As in ordinary mathematical writing, a displayed
   240	formula is part of the surrounding sentence and should be punctuated accordingly.
   241	
   242	Bibliographic entries used only by these notes should live in
   243	\path{docs/paper-gaps/references.bib}.  A new note should ordinarily begin from
   244	\path{docs/paper-gaps/template.tex}, which records the common LaTeX preamble,
   245	the local bibliography, and a model for right-hand source labels in displayed
   246	equations.
   247	
   248	Blueprint prose cites a note like any other source, with
   249	\verb|\cite{gap:<slug>}|; the bibliography entry in
   250	\path{blueprint/src/references.bib} carries the published URL of the note,
   251	whether the note lives in this repository or in another one.  Lean docstrings
   252	and comments use the repository path form \path{docs/paper-gaps/<slug>.tex}.
   253	
   254	The note should then compare the cited source with the informal blueprint, if
   255	there is one, and with the formal statement.  This comparison should be written
   256	in ordinary mathematical prose.  Formal declaration names and source paths should
   257	be supplied only to identify the exact formal statements, and normally belong in
   258	footnotes.
   259	
   260	The conclusion should give a verdict.  It may say that there is no discrepancy,
   261	that the matter is only notational, that an intermediate estimate needs a
   262	harmless correction, that a hypothesis is missing, that there is a theorem-level
   263	gap, or that the question remains open.  The classification should reflect the
   264	mathematics, not the amount of formal work required.
   265	
   266	\section{Decision Principle}
   267	
   268	The formal development should not silently replace the cited assertion by a
   269	different one.  If the formal statement differs from the cited source, the
   270	reason for the difference should be written down.  Conversely, the note should
   271	not overstate the conclusion.  A wrong intermediate scalar is not a fatal gap in
   272	the theorem if the corrected scalar is bounded by the error parameter appearing
   273	in the theorem statement.
   274	
   275	\end{document}

1	# Mathematical Language Guidelines
     2	
     3	MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
     4	the formalization with the paper and blueprint.
     5	
     6	This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
     7	naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
     8	`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.
     9	
    10	## Scope
    11	
    12	These guidelines apply to:
    13	
    14	- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
    15	- module docstrings;
    16	- declaration docstrings;
    17	- documentation-visible section comments;
    18	- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
    19	- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
    20	- issue titles and issue bodies;
    21	- PR titles and PR descriptions.
    22	
    23	## Source of Truth
    24	
    25	Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:
    26	
    27	1. `references/ldt-paper/`
    28	2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
    29	3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files
    30	
    31	When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
    32	example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
    33	projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.
    34	
    35	## Reference Notation And Terminology
    36	
    37	The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
    38	reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
    39	docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
    40	without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.
    41	
    42	When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
    43	location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
    44	first applicable location in the following order:
    45	
    46	1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
    47	   differs from the paper;
    48	2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
    49	   family of declarations in that file;
    50	3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
    51	   blueprint;
    52	4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
    53	   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.
    54	
    55	The explanation should say:
    56	
    57	- the notation or term used in the paper;
    58	- the Lean object or name which represents it;
    59	- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
    60	- the scope in which the replacement should be used.
    61	
    62	A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
    63	where future readers can learn it.
    64	
    65	Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
    66	should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
    67	rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.
    68	
    69	## Naming Norm
    70	
    71	Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
    72	conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
    73	assembled.
    74	
    75	Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
    76	`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
    77	uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
    78	such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
    79	clearer phrase.
    80	
    81	This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
    82	Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
    83	blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
    84	mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
    85	number, or implementation history.
    86	
    87	### Concrete examples
    88	
    89	The table below illustrates the naming norm with examples patterned on the
    90	codebase and on names seen during review.  Some entries are existing names;
    91	others are proposed names for future refactors.  The "avoid" column lists
    92	process-shaped names that encode the history of how the formalization was
    93	assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
    94	paper or blueprint would recognize.
    95	
    96	| Avoid (process-shaped)                        | Prefer (mathematical)                     | Rationale                                              |
    97	|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
    98	| `Line130`                                     | `ProjectiveConsistency`                   | Paper Lemma 5.13, not "the line-130 identity"          |
    99	| `Line169`                                     | `CompletionTransport`                     | Paper Lemma 5.16, step that transports completed data  |
   100	| `Step6`                                       | `Orthonormalization`                      | Paper Section 5, the orthonormalization construction   |
   101	| `FinalAssembly`                               | `DiagonalCompletion`                      | Paper Lemma 5.17, constructing a diagonal POVM         |
   102	| `OneShotIneq`                                 | `SelfConsistencyDataProcessing` (or existing module `Preliminaries.SelfConsistency.DataProcessing`)           | Paper's data-processing inequality for self-consistency |
   103	| `PipelineCheck`                               | `ErrorPropagationBound` (proposed)                   | The bound that propagates error through the test       |
   104	| `QxpLayerWrapper`                             | `ProjectivePOVMCompletion` (proposed)                | The construction from round-projectors to POVMs        |
   105	| `RawSpectralTruncation`                       | `SpectralTruncation`                      | The paper's spectral truncation, not an "unwrapped" version |
   106	| `AddInUStep3To5`                              | `AddInUUpperExcessMass` (proposed)                  | Paper Addendum in §U, the upper excess-mass estimate   |
   107	| `AddInUStep12`                                | `AddInUCommutationTail` (proposed)                   | Paper Addendum in §U, the commutation tail estimate    |
   108	
   109	An avoided name is acceptable only when the cited paper itself uses that
   110	phrase as the mathematical name (e.g., a lemma the paper calls "Step 2").
   111	In that case the docstring should cite the paper's phrasing.
   112	
   113	File-split PRs are a common place where this rule matters: new leaves should be
   114	named by the mathematical boundary they isolate, and any public declarations
   115	exposed by the split should be reviewed under the same standard.
   116	
   117	### Shared helpers
   118	
   119	When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
   120	more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
   121	shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
   122	ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
   123	call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.
   124	
   125	Procedure:
   126	
   127	1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   128	   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   129	   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   130	   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   131	   explicit argument.
   132	2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   133	   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   134	   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   135	   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   136	   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
   137	3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   138	   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
   139	4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   140	   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   141	   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   142	   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   143	   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   144	   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
   145	5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   146	   blueprint location it supports.
   147	
   148	### Legacy identifier treatment
   149	
   150	If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
   151	describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
   152	identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
   153	in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.
   154	
   155	Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
   156	public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
   157	shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
   158	blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.
   159	
   160	## Review Checklist
   161	
   162	Reviewers should use this checklist when examining public names and
   163	documentation prose.  Flag any item that fails.
   164	
   165	- [ ] **Naming.**  Do public declaration names, namespace names, module names,
   166	      theorem field names, and docstring prose describe a mathematical object,
   167	      hypothesis, or conclusion?  Or do they encode the history of how the
   168	      formalization was assembled (paper line numbers, workflow steps,
   169	      implementation-phase labels)?
   170	- [ ] **Source alignment.**  For the mathematical content under review, does
   171	      the prose use the terminology in `references/ldt-paper/` or the
   172	      blueprint?  Are process words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`,
   173	      `raw`, `oneShot`, or `liveBlock` used as mathematical terms when the
   174	      source does not use them that way?
   175	- [ ] **Deviation documented.**  If a Lean name or representation differs from
   176	      the paper, is the deviation documented in a declaration docstring,
   177	      module docstring, blueprint paragraph, or `docs/paper-gaps/` note, in
   178	      that order of preference?
   179	- [ ] **Auxiliary lemmas.**  Are formalization-only auxiliary lemmas introduced
   180	      as such, with prose naming the nearby paper equation, theorem, or
   181	      construction they support?
   182	- [ ] **Shared helpers.**  Does the PR introduce a helper that already exists
   183	      (or near-exists) in another chapter-local leaf?  If so, has it been
   184	      consolidated into a common module with a mathematical name?
   185	- [ ] **Legacy IDs.**  If a legacy Lean identifier is mentioned, is the
   186	      mathematical object described in paper terminology?  If an old public
   187	      identifier cannot be renamed yet, is the required migration recorded in
   188	      the issue, PR description, or an audit file?
   189	- [ ] **Pass-through names.**  Does the PR add an empty pass-through
   190	      abbreviation that introduces a second public name without adding
   191	      mathematical content?  Reject it unless it is a documented compatibility
   192	      wrapper preserving paper-facing or blueprint-facing terminology.
   193	
   194	Review-fix PRs touching a surface covered by an active audit should read the
   195	relevant audit before changing names or prose.
   196
